speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EFFORTS TO OBTAIN RELEASE OF CANADIAN CITIZEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs could inform the house as to the progress that has been made in attempting to persuade the authorities of Czechoslovakia to bring about the release of Mr. Milorad Cop.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EFFORTS TO OBTAIN RELEASE OF CANADIAN CITIZEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that last November I reported on the arrest and subsequent trial of Milorad

Inquiries of the Ministry Cop, a Canadian who was visiting Czechoslovakia. At that time the government was pressing to have an interview with Mr. Cop. This was allowed in January, following completion of the appeal procedure through which his sentence of seven years imprisonment was confirmed.
At the urging of our legation Mr. Cop has been allowed to receive parcels of food, and a further consular visit was arranged. During these interviews it became obvious to our consul that Mr. Cop's health was deteriorating as a result of his confinement. Our serious concern for his health has been brought to the attention of the Czechoslovak authorities on several occasions, and our representations have been broadened on the basis of humanitarian considerations to include a formal request for Mr. Cop's release and return to Canada.
These representations have been through normal diplomatic channels but have been made at a high level in order to emphasize the deep concern of the Canadian government for the welfare of this Canadian citizen. I myself have spoken to the Czechoslovak minister in Ottawa on the subject. Our representations have not thus far had the desired result, but I think we must give the Czechoslovak authorities time to weigh all the factors bearing on this case in the hope that they will eventually recognize the value to our relations of a concrete humanitarian gesture.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PAYMENTS TO PERSONS ATTENDING PRECENSUS SCHOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked whether census takers had received unemployment insurance benefits while taking a course on census matters in Toronto.
I am informed by the unemployment insurance commission that five half day courses were given and that those taking the courses received $5 for each session. This money was considered as earnings by the commission, and after making allowance for the amount which come under permissible earnings the remainder was deducted from the amount of benefit which went to each claimant. In the case of a person whose weekly benefit was $30, if that person had earned $25 through taking these courses, then after the allowable portion of $15 was deducted the remaining $10 would be taken off the benefit and the person would get $20 for that week instead of $30.
This is only an example and, of course, I would not be able to go into further details unless the hon. member is in a position to inform me of the specific case he has in mind, which he has not done as yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CLASSES OF LOANS INCREASING AUTHORIZED CAPITAL, ETC.
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that in my budget speech I said that the government intended to introduce a number of amendments to the Industrial Development Bank Act. With the full support of
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).J
the government the industrial development bank has considerably expanded its operations over the past few years. The measures which are now proposed will further augment significantly and in a variety of ways the ability of the bank to finance the physical expansion of small and medium sized businesses. Moreover, as previously indicated to the house, the bank will be encouraged to assist in increasing measure with the problems which arise in connection with financial consolidation and with changes in ownership.
The proposed amendments will affect almost all phases of the bank's future operations. To begin with, hon. members will be asked to approve a change which will extend the coverage of I.D.B. operations to business enterprises of all types. At present eligibility is restricted to certain classes of business, mainly in the field of manufacturing, processing, mining, logging, construction, transportation, and including part of the service sector of the economy.
The facilities of the bank have grown to the point where it is now feasible to widen the scope of its operations so that enterprises over the whole range of economic activity may be assisted. Of course, the bank will continue to operate with good business judgment and reasonable prudence, and where funds are available from other sources on reasonable terms and conditions, recourse to the bank would be unnecessary. Similarly, it is not expected that the bank will be called upon to use its resources in support of enterprises which can obtain financing under the various governmental measures providing special assistance.
This expansion in coverage, together with the establishment of more branch offices across the country, will undoubtedly lead to an extension of the bank's activities. Moreover, with an intensified effort to bring to the attention of potential borrowers the services which the bank can render, we can confidently expect that the bank will grow in importance as an institution which will further economic growth in general and modernization of Canadian industry in particular.
The experience during the more recent past augurs well for the future, and if the current rate of lending continues, loans made this year will exceed 1,000 in number and $50 million in amount. This expansionary trend, we expect, will become more pronounced in succeeding years. With this in mind it is proposed that parliament provide the bank with additional financing capacity, sufficient to permit it to operate on a substantially larger scale.

First, it is proposed to raise the authorized capital of the bank from the present level of $25 million to $50 million.
Second, parliament will be asked to increase the borrowing authority of the bank. The borrowing authority is now limited to three times the aggregate amount of paid up capital and the reserve fund. Briefly, with paid up capital at a level equal to $25 million and a reserve fund standing at approximately $15 million, this means that the borrowing authority now amounts to about $120 million. It is proposed to increase the limit on borrowing to five times the paid up capital and the reserve fund. As a result and on the basis of a doubling in capital from $25 million to $50 million, the borrowing authority of the bank will reach $325 million. The total resources of the bank, including capital and reserves, will amount to close to $400 million compared with $160 million today. Of course as the reserve fund builds up from the present level of about $15 million we can expect a further increase in the bank's resources.
Hon. members will be aware that at present the act establishes a ceiling of $75 million on the aggregate of individual loans and other commitments which are in excess of $200,000. In line with related changes providing for an enlargement of the resources of the bank, it is proposed to increase this limit to $200 million. As a result the bank will have a potential of approximately $200 million, compared with a current level of $85 million, to cover individual commitments of less than $200,000.
So far I have described changes which will bring more potential borrowers to the doors of the bank and will assure the bank of adequate financial backing for its expanded operations. I am now turning to additional measures which are designed to enhance the performance of the bank in a qualitative rather than a quantitative way. The preamble of the act establishing the industrial development bank states the objectives to be pursued by this institution. These objectives relate to the promotion of the economic welfare of Canada, and to this end the bank may lend or may guaranteee loans to business enterprises, may enter into underwriting agreements and may engage in equity financing. It is surely appropriate that at this time, when every effort is being made to increase the usefulness of the bank, attention should also be paid to the adequacy of the existing powers of the bank in rendering financial assistance.
Based on actual experience, it is found that such powers as the bank now has should be broadened in two specific ways. First, it is
90205-6-462J
Industrial Development Bank Act proposed to facilitate bank action in cases where financial assistance is required for the purchase of movables. Accordingly, it is intended that the bank be authorized to acquire title to movable property, such as machinery and equipment, and to make it available to a borrower by means of a conditional sales agreement. This should prove helpful to borrowers under circumstances where it would be either impossible or cumbersome to take chattel mortgage security on movables and where purchase by the bank, subject to redemption by the borrower, proves to be a most efficient and most convenient way of rendering financial assistance.
A second amendment will permit the bank to make funds available in respect of transportation equipment, for instance trucks and buses, through the purchase of equipment trust certificates. Hon. members will be aware that it is fairly common practice to finance the acquisition of transportation equipment through the issue by a trust company of such certificates or obligations. The proposed extension of the powers of the bank will improve the flexibility of its operations and make it easier for the bank to participate in arrangements for the financing of transportation equipment.
In keeping with the expansion in the scope and functions of the industrial development bank, the amendments will also make provision for the enlargement of the board of directors and of the executive committee to include not only the deputy minister of finance as at present but also the deputy minister of trade and commerce. Provision has also been made for a second director from the business community to be added to the executive committee.
It will be evident that the proposed amendments to the Industrial Development Bank Act, which I have outlined in summary form, will enable that institution to provide more and better services to small and medium sized businesses. I have also referred to the contributions which the industrial development bank can make in cases where enterprises, particularly small firms and family concerns, are faced with problems which, for their solution, require the infusion of new management and new capital. Some of these difficulties arise as a result of the general competitive trend in our economy; others relate to the impact of estate taxes. In such situations the industrial development bank can play an increasingly active and constructive role by making funds available as well as technical assistance on a variety of managerial problems. As indicated in the

Industrial Development Bank Act budget speech, it is the hope of the government that in this way the industrial development bank can also contribute to the retention in Canada of the ownership and control of Canadian businesses.
The bank has been furnishing a valuable service in providing for the financial needs of small and medium sized businesses which, because of their size, find it difficult to raise capital on the security market. The amendments which are before the house now will enable the bank to play an increasingly useful role in the future by assisting private enterprise to provide more employment and develop a stronger, more productive and more flexible economy.

Mr. Chairman, there is no reason why we on this side should delay the passage of this resolution, which embodies certain amendments to be made to the Industrial Development Bank Act. We shall have an opportunity to deal with this matter when the bill is before the house. In any event, we on this side have been advocating for some time now an expansion of the functions and activities of this very useful piece of machinery through proposals which we have made, some of which are referred to in the resolution and in the statement the minister has just made, though not all.
We think the bank has performed, as I have just said, very useful services. We think it should be given, as is proposed, greater financial resources, and that its functions and activities should be broadened. We feel especially that it should be given greater responsibilities and greater opportunities to assist in regional economic development, where government assistance to small business is particularly necessary and desirable for, among other things, employment reasons. We think the industrial development bank could, if it were given the opportunity, play a very useful part in this field. We have gone further, I gather, than the government proposes to go in these amendments, and have suggested that the bank should be separated in its administration from the Bank of Canada and be given a separate corporate existence.
I think that is all I need to say about the resolution at this stage. We will be able to examine the bill when it is introduced, and perhaps further discussion will be required then.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group want to expedite the passage of this resolution. We too are very happy to see the expansion of the industrial development bank. We note that even last year there was a 24 per cent increase in the number and a 26 per cent increase in the amount of the loans made

We are particularly happy to see that the small businessman will have greater opportunity and that the scope of the bank is going to be extended especially to the service industries, which I think are going to become more and more important in Canada.
As I said, we are not in the least going to hold up the passage of this resolution. However, I should like to read the preamble to the Industrial Development Bank Act, because I think it has an important relation to what we are doing today:
Whereas it is desirable to establish an industrial development bank to promote the economic welfare of Canada by increasing the effectiveness of monetary action through ensuring the availability of credit to industrial enterprises-
Here, I think, is the important part.
-which may reasonably be expected to prove successful if-
This is a very important "if".

a high level of national income and employment is maintained .. .
I think this is something which should be very much in the mind of the minister as he seeks to improve this bank; that this act was passed in the expectation that there would be a high level of national income and especially a high level of employment. It is rather strange that we are now turning the whole thing backwards. Now we are depending on the industrial development bank to create the employment so that the bank itself can be successful. I think this is something which might be in the mind of the minister as he brings forward this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the passage of the resolution, but there are some things I should like to say because I feel very strongly on this subject. Ever since I was elected to the house many small industries that have been trying to establish themselves have come to me for some assistance. I believe that in the past the industrial development bank has not been carrying out the duty for which it was originally intended; at least if I have understood correctly the comments that have been made to me over the years regarding this duty, this is what I have learned. I believe that the bank has been operating on too restrictive a basis.

Obviously the bank was limited to some extent by the statute which confined it to the type of business set out in the act, and I am very pleased to see that the resolution and the bill to follow will enlarge the types of business which will qualify for assistance under the Industrial Development Bank Act.
Those types of business were too restricted, and in my opinion the restrictions were applied too strictly. I know of several businesses that tried to get loans and, although they seemed to have good prospects, for one technical reason or another the applications were delayed and in many cases refused. It has been felt that while the industrial development bank was set up to assist small businesses and small industries to get started, it has been too much of a bankers' bank and has not been performing the function for which it was originally intended. I have two or three examples I should like to give where I feel that the industrial development bank could very well have stepped right in and done the job for which it was intended.
A couple of years ago an industry in South River in my constituency had good market prospects for its product. They applied for assistance to the industrial development bank and were turned down for various reasons. Perhaps I was not aware of all of them, but certainly some assistance to this business would certainly have kept it going.
There is another case in which I have been very interested. In the village of McKellar near Parry Sound a man by the name of Stroud, who is an inventor of printing press machines, has achieved a major break-through in the printing trade. He has constructed a prototype of a printing press that has been examined by people from Sweden, Germany and the United States. He has been most anxious to build his press in Canada if he can. Excellent opportunities have been made available to him by people who would buy the patent and manufacture the machine outside of Canada. For some time he has been trying to get financial assistance from the industrial development bank. I believe that eventually he would get some assistance, because he has been making good progress. However, in my opinion the present amendment will help him to produce in Canada for export a very good, marketable product. It has been examined by responsible authorities, who say that not only can it be sold in Canada but it also can be exported to all parts of the world.
For that reason I welcome this assistance. This gentleman has been trying for two years to get his product on the road. I have been doing the best I could to assist him within the restrictions placed on such assistance by the industrial development bank, and

There are 264 other members here in the house, and I have no doubt that every one of them has similar examples of projects that could be mentioned in respect of which financing is too limited and where a little bit of a push is needed in order to get started. The idea is there, the ability is there, but the finances are not.
There was one other matter I wanted to mention, Mr. Chairman. I should like to refer to the power of the industrial development bank to assist in financing projects by the purchase of stock in a company. Some of the people who have approached me have said, why could not the government back us

Industrial Development Bank Act up by taking over our plant and developing our markets, and when the thing is running turn it back to us? Would that not be a reasonable procedure? The government is interested in the development of Canadian products. Would it not be reasonable for the government to take over the project, provide people from the technical branches of government to assist in financing and in export arrangements, in production of the machine and in research; then, when the project is fully developed, turn it back to us. Well, of course, the difficulty in this procedure is that the government would take all the risk and the private individual would be in a position to take the profit. There is power in the Industrial Development Bank Act to come into the field, purchase stock in a company for long enough to get it going, and give it the necessary financial backing. Then the stock can be sold to the public. I think this is the type of thing that would be very, very useful. When I spoke previously about the Stroud printing press, there was some publicity about it and several people from other countries approached me as to the method that might be used in financing. I found that several countries in Europe followed the procedure of the government giving assistance through stock purchases. The government purchased the major part of the stock and carried out the development, and when the company was on its feet and ready to go into the market and export, they sold the stock back to the public. The company was sold to the public for whatever it was worth. If a good job had been done in designing and producing a plant, the stock was worth something. The people who purchase it are interested in the development. If the job has not been done so well, then the stock is down and the government fund will have to take a loss. The reason the government fund has to take a loss is that it was an investment. However, I believe it is better that they should take a loss in this way and pass it on to the people who purchase the stock, than merely to take a loss on a bad investment by way of a loan.
I suggest that the industrial development bank take full advantage of the provisions in the act at the present time which would enable it to do this type of financing. Direct loans are certainly a good thing, but they do have to be paid back. Interest has to be paid, and so forth. The stock financing arrangement does not require payments of any kind from
[Mr. Aiken. 1

the company. The government which has purchased the stock merely sells it again to the public, and there is no obligation on the company to repay a large outstanding loan. I certainly suggest that this type of assistance would be very beneficial both to the development of new industries in Canada and to the export of those products which are made in this country and which can be exported.
I note, Mr. Chairman, that the resolution does not propose alterations in this type of financing and I see no reason why there should be a change. I believe that the type of financing to which I have referred has not been taken advantage of sufficiently, though the powers are already there. The resolution does refer to a provision to enable the bank to take title to movable property and make the property available to the operator under a conditional sales agreement. I believe this is an additional power.
I believe these are all the remarks I wish to make on this particular resolution, Mr. Chairman, except that I am glad to see not only an increase in the funds available but also a widening of the class which will qualify under this act, as well as the intention to make reasonable use of the authority which the industrial development bank already has. In my opinion a good deal of the difficulty has not been that the bank has not had the power but that the bank has not been using it. I suggest that the enlargement of the bank's powers under this resolution, along with the full use of the powers the bank already has, would enable a great deal to be done to encourage industry in this country, to provide a improved level of employment and to increase our exports of those items we produce in Canada, thus reversing the trend of imports from other countries of goods we cannot produce in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some brief remarks on this item. I was glad to see today on the other side of the house indications of general concurrence with regard to the changed plan for the industrial development bank. I should like to comment on some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. He mentioned the rather restrictive nature of the bank's regulations in the past. I think this has indeed been so. We have many medium and small sized enterprises scattered throughout my riding of Halton, a number of which have been interested at various times in obtaining funds from the industrial development bank. Nevertheless, while some companies have been successful, may have been turned down.
The criticism has been made that this was indeed a sort of bankers' bank. We have heard

the same criticism of this bank as we have of ordinary banks, namely that if you wanted a loan you practically had to have the capital you needed before the loan would be made. As one hon. member has said, you really have to prove you do not need the loan before you can obtain it. This is a very fundamental problem which has been applicable to the industrial development bank in the past, and I hope some change will be made in the future. We realize that a complete change in the other direction would not be possible, but we would hope for more flexibility.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has cited various firms and industries in his riding which have benefited or would benefit fro mthe operations of this bank. I have in my riding various firms engaged in new aspects of plastics, new aircraft firms and other imaginative new industries which would welcome, and I am sure are welcoming, the changed provisions which are to be brought about. These new industries, these applications of new methods to old industries, are a most important part of our Canadian development in the modernization of business in our country in its competitive struggle both within Canada and with various foreign countries.
I would like to stress that the industrial development bank could in the future pay more attention to new ideas, I mean ideas in the sense of people or companies that perhaps may not have the risk capital or the background in property to develop their inventions, their new methods and their ideas. From a banking standpoint this may be difficult indeed to evaluate, but surely there is scope somewhere in our government field for an agency or body, perhaps indeed within the industrial development bank, to be just a little more risky in its approach to conventional banking methods with respect to new ideas or processes.
As the previous speaker stated, it so often happens in this country that such new methods, such new approaches to industry, may leave Canada both in ownership and in application because of the lack of risk capital. Generally they go to the United States. I have seen many instances of this. I hope that in future the changed provisions of the bank will provide for the retention in Canada of more of these new ideas. I am sure they are necessary to enable us to modernize and become more competitive in the world around us.
Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition mentioned increased facilities of the industrial development bank in various regions of Canada. I did not hear him develop that idea further. Perhaps we could hear that at some future date. It is difficult to visualize just how that might be done under the present
Industrial Development Bank Act circumstances. We understand that the industrial development bank is going to increase the scope of the industries and companies which it may service. Indeed, service industries and service companies are to come within the field of its coverage.
Another area which has been mentioned by hon. members, and which is a most important one, concerns small family companies, Canadian businesses in origin, management and ownership, which for various reasons are in danger of passing into foreign control. I have seen this happen in various towns in my area and indeed, speaking from slight knowledge, in many small and medium sized towns throughout southern Ontario. I refer to family businesses perhaps established 25, 50 or 100 years ago, with two, three or four generations of Canadian ownership, really pioneer families in those areas, and perhaps businesses upon which many of the people of the town or region in which they are located depend for employment. Many of these businesses are being bought and control is being obtained by United States companies and individuals.
We welcome the statement of the minister that the bank will play an increasing part in assisting the present Canadian ownership through the problems of estate taxes, through the transition perhaps from one generation to another, and indeed the aspect which the minister has emphasized, of technical advice to be given to such companies. This technical and advisory help has presumably been given in the past to some extent, but I gather from the minister's comments that the technical and advisory aspect of the industrial development bank will be increased in the future. I presume this may assist such companies, particularly in the transition stage of ownership which occurs in many small firms.
We welcome the figures for the past year or so in connection with the bank; the fact that their loans increased by a very definite percentage last year; that the indications for the present year are that perhaps a total of 1,000 loans will be made. We are looking forward even more to the future because of the announced changes; the increase in authorized capital from $25 million to $50 million, and the increase in borrowing authority as described by the minister earlier today, to a total of $225 million. The total of these provisions will very greatly increase the ability of the bank to assist Canadian industry.
Another subject which was touched upon in this connection concerns modernization of existing industries. It seems that on many occasions firms which have been successful in the past, and perhaps are today, need to expend a very considerable amount of capital

This sort of thing is within the purview of the bank, and it is to be hoped that the industrial development bank will take an aggressive stand in assisting industries in these very necessary changes. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise for a few moments to congratulate the Minister of Finance on this measure, which is one more of the many measures he has put forward to stimulate and develop the Canadian economy. In the past in this house I have had occasion to be critical of the industrial development bank, but I notice that in recent years they have been extending their loans and making more loans, particularly in my own Atlantic region. I very much hope this trend will continue, and that credit facilities through the industrial development bank will be easier. At the moment there is a file on my desk in my office concerning a new industry which proposes to move into the town of Inverness in my riding. I know the location of this industry there will only be possible through assistance and through the special financing which is available from agencies of the nature of the industrial development bank.
I suggest one further step which might be taken toward the development of the Canadian economy. I have in mind the expansion of the industrial development bank for the


purpose of or the setting up of a new agency on a national basis for the location of new industries in this country. I am sure there are many industries abroad which would establish branches in Canada if there were some agency organized on a federal basis to invite them to settle here and assist them in their financing. There are, of course, parallel agencies operating successfully in a number of the provinces. In Nova Scotia the Industrial Estates Limited organization and the provincial industrial development fund have been successful in the last few years in establishing new industry, in expanding existing industries, and in keeping within the province industries which might otherwise have moved to other regions.
However, settlement agencies of the nature of Industrial Estates Limited are necessarily limited in scope, inasmuch as they work under provincial authority only and their funds are limited to what the province can provide. I would think that federal agencies similar to those which are now working in the provinces would be most helpful in bringing big industry to Canada, operations which might be beyond the scope and resources of provincial organizations.
I have in mind, for example, that on the North American continent there is no factory which makes small, low cost automobiles, yet there is a wide market in this hemisphere for automobiles of this type which would not be in competition with cars produced for sale at higher prices. It has been suggested to me that Nova Scotia would be an ideal site for a factory manufacturing low cost cars. A factory of this kind would have to look to the whole hemisphere for its market. Indeed, it would have to look across the world in order to sell its products, and it would be of great advantage for it to be situated on tidewater so that cheap transportation would be available.
Moreover, there is on Cape Breton island a good modern steel plant. It is efficiently run and produces a good product, but it is operating under a handicap in that most of its product must be transported to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario for sale. Thus, added to the cost of producing steel is this extra cost of transportation. If there were some way in which a large industry could be settled close to that mill to take advantage of the coal and the steel which is available, it would give a considerable boost to the whole maritime region.
It may, of course, not be feasible to establish a low cost automobile plant in that area, but all the necessary resources would seem to be there, and this is the type of project I should like to see investigated. It would have to be considered with a view to

bringing in men with the special managerial and technical skills required to make use of these resources, and all this would involve large scale national financing.
This is a project of a type which perhaps, lies beyond the resources of Industrial Estates Limited in the province. It involves big industry in a day when big industry and mass production are becoming increasingly important. I should like to see a federal agency established whose responsibility it would be to assist in the founding of new industries which could properly and feasibly operate in Canada, and which would be responsible for attempting to bring into regions such as my own industries which would be suited to the resources and economy of those areas.
An agency of this type should, of course, work closely with provincial agencies to set up better facilities for research into the types of industry which could be located in various parts of Canada. It could also assist in bringing in people with executive and managerial skills whose specialized knowledge would be required in connection with the establishment of such industries.
The nation has grown very well under our private enterprise system. We have a high standard of living, and we sell our products across the world. However, I am sure there are many other products which we could be producing and I am sure, too, hon. members will appreciate that there are some areas of Canada which are not growing as fast as they should, chiefly because under the private enterprise system money or business interests cannot be as easily found to settle industries in those regions. I should like to see a special agency set up whose duty it would be to consider ways of encouraging industrialization in areas such as the maritimes. Such an agency would work in co-operation with the provincial agencies which have already been established.
To me it seems a shame that we should have a steel fabricating centre on the island of Cape Breton, together with a large amount of fuel in the area, but that we should only be able to move this steel as a raw material to other parts of Canada for processing. At the moment there is under consideration the establishment of a cold rolling mill at Contre-coeur on the St. Lawrence river for the processing of Sydney steel. The establishment of this rolling mill would be of assistance to the Sydney mill. However, if an industry such as an automobile industry could be established in the maritime area I am sure Dosco would consider it very feasible to establish their cold rolling mill in that area. Around the steel mill at Sydney there could be built up an industrial complex

speechtext:
I should like to thank hon. members in all parts of the committee for the support they have expressed for this measure. There are three points with which I think I should deal briefly before the resolution is reported.
The Leader of the Opposition raised a point at the outset of his remarks concerning the separation of the industrial development bank from the Bank of Canada. I wish to make it clear that while this measure does not propose that separation, I would not wish it thought that this suggestion is eliminated for all time. The proposal has been made from various quarters from time to time. It has been considered by the government, and it will continue to be under consideration.
A good deal will depend upon the views of management and the bank authorities. There are some problems which would arise if such a proposal were put into effect. I do not need to detain the committee now by reviewing this subject. I simply wish to make the point that this proposal has been advanced from several quarters, and is not dismissed from consideration simply because it is not included within the scope of the present bill. We shall continue to examine this matter.
Second, a point was raised about using the bank's operations with a view to regional considerations. I think it should be stressed again, particularly in the light of the desirability of extending the development of secondary industry in the Atlantic area, that as far as the government is concerned it is our view that the resources of the bank should be available for this purpose. Indeed, the expansion in the number of branch offices of the industrial development bank throughout Canada has been designed to make the bank and its facilities as serviceable as possible to all regions of the country. The number of branch offices of the bank in 1955 was only four. That number was increased by 1960 to 13, and the bank is now better able than ever before to give regional services in different parts of the country.
I think it will be in the minds of all hon. members that it is desirable that these services should be available with as much local accommodation as possible in those areas of the country which have not heretofore enjoyed the same advantages in the development of secondary industries as have some of the more centrally located parts of the country. I can assure hon. members, and particularly the hon. member who last spoke,

Industrial Development Bank Act that the facilities of the bank are intended to be available to serve the worthy object of assisting in the development of secondary industries in the Atlantic area of this country.
The third and last point which I should like to mention, Mr. Chairman, concerns the scope of operations of the bank. This point has been mentioned and I do not wish to repeat what I said earlier. However, one hon. member inquired whether there is any intention that the facilities of the bank should be available on terms which simply duplicate the credit facilities available through other institutions, for example the chartered banks. Let me make it very clear that the industrial development bank is not intended to duplicate existing facilities in this respect. That would not be a proper function of such an institution provided with government resources and government sponsorship. Indeed, the statute is very clear on that point. Section 15 of the act, in subsection 1, contains the following provisions:
Subject to section 14-
Section 14 concerns the aggregate of liabilities.
-where in the opinion of the board-
Or of an officer authorized for that purpose by the board.
(a)	a person is engaged or about to engage in an industrial enterprise in Canada-
I hope you will note the terms of the next clause, Mr. Chairman.
(b)	credit or other financial resources would not otherwise be available on reasonable terms and conditions-
It has been the policy of parliament, from the time this institution was brought into existence by the legislation of the 1944-45 session, that the services and facilities should not duplicate those provided by other institutions under private ownership. The industrial development bank was intended to be a lender in the secondary sense, providing credit particularly in the medium and longer term field not otherwise available to industries. The advantages offered by the act were obviously largely directed to the smaller and medium sized businesses which are not in a position to go into the security market to meet their capital requirements, or borrowing requirements on a scale not justifying resort to the capital market. I think the situation is quite clear in that regard, and has been from the outset of this institution and the legislation governing it, and the bill now before the committee makes no change in that regard.
I thank all hon. members for the support they have expressed for this measure. It is

refreshing to bring in a measure which has the general support of all sections of the house.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

If that is the case, Mr. Chairman, the point that I made is no longer valid. I should like to comment now on the resolution which the minister has discussed. So far as we on this side of the house are concerned there will not be the slightest difficulty with regard to our approving the resolution and the bill to follow. The reasons for that are quite clear.
For many years now the Liberal party has stood committed to the construction of this line. I remember that when I occupied the position now held by my hon. friend the construction of this railway was under consideration, and after I left and my successor, the Hon. Mr. Marler, took over the Department of Transport I know that the matter was also under active consideration then.
Canadian National Railways, both when I held the office and after I left, was of the opinion that this railway was essential to the development of the north. In their view the railway was essential if the base metal deposits in that area were to be developed. The committee will probably remember that on a number of occasions resolutions were put out on the order paper demanding approval of the construction of this railway. In 1957 the hon. member for Mackenzie River had a resolution on the order paper in these terms:
That in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability of recommending the construction as soon as possible of a railway from Grimshaw, Alberta, to the south shore of Great Slave lake, Northwest Territories, in order to open up and develop the agricultural lands of northern Alberta and the vast mineral and oil resources of the Northwest Territories.
I think all of the reasons given by the minister for the construction of this railway can be found in the brief which was presented to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by Mr. R. G. Robertson, commissioner of the Northwest Territories, at Edmonton, Alberta, on November 22, 1955. At page 24 of that brief the commissioner stated:
May I submit for the consideration of the commission three methods by which transportation facilities into the Northwest Territories might be improved. The first is the construction of a railroad to Great Slave lake.

In the following pages are found all the reasons for the construction of this line, reasons which have already been enunciated by the minister in the statement he made a moment ago. One will find here a discussion of the base metals that would be developed as a result of the construction of the railway, a discussion of the forest reserves that would be tapped by the railway, together with the benefits that would ensue from base metal developments and sales. There is also consideration of the amount of ensuing freight. There is a further statement which the minister stressed particularly in his remarks a moment ago, that the line was to be built to carry lead and zinc concentrates and also, but more particularly, for the purpose of northern development.
The brief which I hold in my hand, reads in part at page 29 as follows:
A railway to Great Slave lake will not be just another railway. It is not a railway to a lake, or to open a mine or to serve a community. A railway to Great Slave lake will be one of the great development railroads of the country.
Then, the brief goes on to develop that idea. Without in any way minimizing or taking away from the minister's statement, therefore, I simply say that as far back as 1955 there was brought to the attention of the royal commission on economic prospects the need for the construction of this railway, and the vital assistance it would be to the development of metals and the development of the whole north country.
I should like to remind the minister and the committee that the construction of this railway was advocated in the Pearson plan, the plan which was put forward in our election platform in 1958. It is regarded that, unfortunately, there has been a considerable delay on the part of the government in the construction of this line which was first announced in the speech from the throne several years ago. It was announced a second time, and then there was an announcement that a royal commission would determine which of the two routes would be followed, that from Waterways north or from the end of rail on the western route, from Grimshaw. When the royal commission reported on which of these two alternatives would be more advantageous, the government included in its last speech from the throne, that is the one in 1960, the announcement that a location survey would be made. The location survey, I understand, has not yet been completed, as the minister indicated during consideration of his estimates. Nevertheless, the legislation is now being brought forward.
We agree with the minister that this will be a great step forward in the development of the north and in the development of the
Canadian National Railways resources in the north, and it will have also the advantage of bringing about the completion of an important link in defence establishments in northern Canada. We see no reason why we on this side of the house should not give this resolution our wholehearted support.

Mr. Chairman, this is an important resolution covering a very interesting development, having in mind further development in the north. Before proceeding, I cannot help but comment that it is very interesting to members of this group to note how quickly these large and successful private companies, such as Consolidated Mining and Smelting, come running to the government with cap in hand to get public funds to assist them with their free enterprise. The Canadian Pacific Railway has controlling interest in Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. My inquirers want to know why the Canadian Pacific did not undertake construction of this required railroad without having the company in question come to the government for public assistance. I understand that the building of this railroad was primarily prompted by representations made by the directors of Consolidated Mining and Smelting to this and former governments. In addition to carrying lead and zinc to the smeltering trade I understand, according to the minister's report, that there are tremendous quantities of forest products to be transported over this line. There are the possibilities of great agricultural developments.
I am not going to take much time now because I think the debate on this question could take place very satisfactorily on second reading. However, I do suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this proposal contains financial, economic and technical implications of major importance that require careful study by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for the protection of the public. I believe this bill should go to the committee for a complete study. The committee should bring before it the president of the Canadian Pacific, or some suitable official, the president of the Canadian National or a suitable official, the president of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, as well as officials of the Department of National Revenue to say how income tax arrangements are provided for under these circumstances. Before we pass the bill finally, we should be able to go back to our constituencies secure in the knowledge that we can defend this resolution, having received all the information we sought. Mr. Chairman, let me at once take issue with the statement made by the last speaker that the motive and the reason for this resolution and what is behind it springs primarily from the interest and the request of the directors of a mining company. The background of this project comes primarily from the demands and requests expressed over a period of 30 to 35 years by thousands of people, small people, the homesteaders, the settlers, the pioneers in the north area of my constituency; the people who

went into the Northwest Territories and who have established communities, cities and towns there. They are the individuals who are responsible for this particular project. They are the people who have requested this project, a request to which this government has given heed. I say that the hon. member's statement is entirely at variance with the facts.
I agree with the hon. member for Laurier who said that this project was one which had long been promised. It had been promised for almost 30 years. This promise has finally been fulfilled. It has been fulfilled by this government under the right hon. gentleman whose interest in and concern for the rights of the small man are well known to the people of this country. This is a project realized only after this government took office. It is a project that, true enough, was promised for many, many years under the previous administration but which did not get beyond the stage of promise.
I would hope this matter could be considered, and I believe it will be, in a nonpartisan manner. It is my genuine belief that this is a project not of a local or parochial nature, but one which many years after the interests of the mining people may be exhausted will be of benefit and value to the economy and to the people of this nation far beyond what was conceived in the first place.
I listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier with regard to the statement made to the royal commission on economic affairs, commonly known as the Gordon commission. A brief was presented by Mr. Gordon Robertson, the deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources. I quoted that same statement in the first speech I made in this house to lend emphasis to the necessity for this particular project.
I should like to make this statement, Mr. Chairman, before I deal with some other aspects of this particular matter. There has been some delay in carrying out this project but I would point out to the hon. member for Laurier and to hon. members of this committee that the entire responsibility for this delay can be laid at the door of the previous administration, because for reasons which are completely unintelligible to me, which reasons were advanced and which on examination were shown to be based on completely fallacious assumptions, they sought to divert what was the natural and the logical course of the route of this railway to one which would have proved calamitous for this nation; a route which would have involved the expenditure of a far greater sum than would have been justified in a project of this nature; a route which, in my humble opinion-which is reinforced by the findings

of the royal commission, to which I will refer later-should not have been followed.
It was only because the previous administration sought to divert what was the natural route to this other route that this delay occurred. I established this when I spoke on the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I put upon the record facts which constitute an irrebuttable circumstantial case reinforced by documents and references and buttressed by citations which to me indicate that these facts cannot be denied. This was the situation this government faced when it come into office and to which I will refer later.
I think I would be derelict in my duty, Mr. Chairman, if I did not at this time pay tribute to those who have assisted in the realization and consummation of this project which they so devoutly desired. These people have worked for so long to this end. I refer to the thousands of people in the area of Peace River and in the Northwest Territories, many of whom would at first blush appear to have no interest at all in this great project; people living 200 and 300 miles away; people coming from a land which had for so many years been so bitterly disappointed on so many occasions with respect to promises of transportation facilities that they felt this was their fight. This was a project to which they committed themselves irrespective of their personal or pecuniary interests. I refer to the boards of trade, the chambers of commerce, the farmers union organizations and the individuals who worked with me in preparing the material which was submitted to government and to commissions. There is a debt of gratitude owing to these people.
I would also like to refer to the position taken by my colleague the hon. member for Athabasca, who comes from an area which is to some extent involved in this particular issue. The hon. member took what I can only regard as being a proper, worthy and statesmanlike position. His views as expressed in this house from time to time were that this issue should be decided upon the facts, which were shown to be in the interests of Canada as a whole. In doing that, the hon. member is deserving of commendation. I also pay my respects to the hon. member for Mackenzie River, who has long been a doughty and a strong fighter for the things which are requisite and desirable for the people of the Northwest Territories.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I want to pay tribute to the government and to the Prime Minister. When I first came to Ottawa in 1958 I found a situation which presented some very formidable aspects. So far as I could see, decisions had been made under the previous administration which indicated that the
Canadian National Railways natural and proper aspirations of the people in my part of the country were going to be neglected. With that in mind I presented petitions; I spoke in the house; I presented to the cabinet and to the Prime Minister the request of the people of my area. In his consideration of this particular problem the Prime Minister was not in any way partisan or biased. All that we asked was that this issue should be judged fairly and properly on the facts; on the true, accurate and relevant facts.
We asked for the appointment of a board or tribunal which would make an impartial, equitable inquiry into this issue. That request was granted by the government and there was established in due course a royal commission to make inquiry into this route. That was the Manning commission. It was as a result of the findings of that commission that we have the resolution which is now before the committee. If it had not been for the position taken by the Prime Minister and the government that there was a case which must be heard, I fear that the result might well have been that, as I said earlier, we would have been embarking upon this project on a basis which might well have been disastrous.
I thoroughly agree with what has been hinted at by the hon. member for Kootenay West. There are railway problems facing us today, and I think we must examine this issue quite closely and quite carefully. Fortunately, in doing so we can direct our attention to information, facts, figures and statements which have been gathered by the Manning royal commission. This commission sat for almost a year and its decision was finally made after several months' consideration. This to a large extent accounted for the delay in introducing this resolution. Comment was made at one time that the findings of the commission were not the findings of the majority. I must make reference to this matter. This is altogether incorrect. The findings of the commission were based on a two to one majority in favour of the railroad being constructed on the route established by this resolution. I do not propose to go into what was said, but I want to make it clear beyond doubt that when the commission filed its recommendation two of the commissioners came to the conclusion that the western route, or the route to Grim-shaw, should be selected.
We have recently had the benefit of reading the first report of the MacPherson commission dealing with the difficulties of the railways in Canada. I think therefore it is logical that members of this committee will be concerned to examine this question in the light

Canadian National Railways of what will probably be the economic benefits to the people in the northern part of the Peace River region, in the Northwest Territories and in Canada as a whole. I should like to give the committee certain facts and figures which I think will be helpful when we come to second reading. The question of timber was mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West. At the time the Manning royal commission held its hearings the province of Alberta was interested in this matter and we have the benefit of an extensive study and assessment of the potential yield on a perpetual yearly basis from the area which may be called tributary to the route which this railway is to adopt. This information is set out at page 86 of the first volume of the report.
After studying the whole matter carefully, after obtaining the reports of people engaged in the lumber business in the area and after going through the minute and accurate reports of the forestry department of Alberta the commission came up with this information. They found there was a total volume of saw logs which could be converted into lumber amounting to 8 billion board feet. Of course, we must look at this from the viewpoint of the railway in an attempt to find out what revenue can be expected from the various types of traffic which the road can carry. This total volume of timber is expressed as an annual cut of 136 million board feet which would provide a total of 4,500 cars or a total revenue of $3,600,000. I am not suggesting, and I do not expect the committee to accept, that this will be realized at once but it is the potential as far as saw logs are concerned. The total which the area would yield to the railway in board feet would bring an annual revenue of $3,600,000.
Going on to the question of pulp, there is sufficient potential in the area to justify in the course of time the construction of six 500-ton pulp mills at 200 million f.b.m. per annum resulting in a potential annual tonnage of 200,000 tons a year with a total rail revenue of $12 million. This, too, I do not expect will be realized for some time. However, it undoubtedly represents the opinion of people who have examined this situation closely with a view to determining the quantity of freight which will be available to this railway when it has been constructed and the development has taken place which we who live in the area know will, in fact, happen.
I turn from this to agriculture. During the last few weeks anxiety has been felt by many people in western Canada and, for that matter all over the country with respect to the grievous situation in the farm lands of western Canada and parts of the western


states of the United States. We have heard, in addition, of the situation in China where large regions are said to be threatened with famine. All this must give pause to all those who have in the past said we shall never require more land to be opened up and added to our existing farm acreage. I think he would be a brave man who, in the light of natural uncertainties and in the light of the speed at which the population of the world is expanding, would say that in the normal course of development we would not require the farm land which will become available after this railroad has been constructed.
While gathering information in connection with the brief I presented to the royal commission I had occasion to seek advice from the agriculture department of the province of Alberta which put out a number of sheets covering various areas. On one occasion
1	found there were in a certain number of townships in which were alleged to be approximately 400,000 acres of potential farm land. Within a year of the time I first obtained that information until the time I presented my views to the royal commission, that 400,000 acres had been expanded to over
2	million. There is no doubt there will be tributary to the route this railway will take, from a minimum of 5 million acres to a maximum of 9 million acres of potential farm land. It is my sincere conviction that in due course, with the development of our country the agricultural production from that land will be required in Canada and elsewhere.
May I reassure hon. members that we are not thinking in terms of wheat production. What we expect this land will yield will be the oilseeds, the grasses, the feeds-the type of mixed and versatile farming for the products of which there always has been and, I believe, there always will be a proper market. This land will come into production and the production will be required by the world.
I could go into the subject of gas and oil. The whole area is permeated by a development scheme being undertaken at the present time by oil companies which are actively engaged in explorations for natural gas and oil. There are some minor fields already in existence. I have every reason to believe that before the end of the next few years major fields will be discovered in the area. We do not need a railway primarily for gas and oil development but we shall need a railway if in the course of the development of natural gas and oil resources we find there are large quantities of natural gas which have to be processed, resulting in the availability of sulphur.

Some mention of minerals has been made by the minister. True enough, Pine Point minerals, one of the largest lead-zinc bodies in the world, will come into production with a minimum of some 220,000 tons of lead and zinc concentrates a year. That is the minimum. I have no doubt at all that it will be substantially extended.
I noted in a recent press report appearing in the Edmonton Journal that the president of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company felt that this would justify the expenditure of some $20 million at Pine Point alone. I have also been informed by a reasonably good authority that there will be a commensurate expenditure of almost the same amount of money in and around Trail in due course in order to take advantage of the extra concentrates which will be moved into that area.
With the minimum tonnage at which the railway will commence hauling there will be a yield to the railway of something in the neighbourhood of $1 million to $1.5 million per year. That, of course, is subject to such agreements as are referred to in the resolution which will be negotiated in the best interests of the people of Canada by this government.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something about the benefits of this railroad to the people of the Northwest Territories. Since 1937-38 when mining commenced in Yellowknife and district the people of that area have been carrying on with an economy which has been unfortunately hampered by the tremendously large costs of bringing freight into and out of that area. I have a table before me which is part of the first report of the Manning royal commission regarding present freight rates and expected freight rates once this railroad has been constructed. At the present time, based on class 45 carload lots by rail, class 5 for carload lots by barge, and class 4 for truckload lots by truck, the cost is $3.68 per hundred pounds from Edmonton to Yellowknife via Grimshaw and Hay River, and $4.68 by highway using the winter rate. That latter figure will have to be reduced because at the present time the highway to Yellowknife has been completed. Set against that are the figures which have been given to the commission which will represent the rates after the railway is built, a rate of $2.61. One can therefore appreciate that there will be a very substantial saving as a result of this railway being built.
In respect to the situation which exists in the Northwest Territories, I suggest that the area is on the verge of tremendous development, but in order for that development to
Canadian National Railways proceed, the people there must be in a position to receive their commodities at a rate which will permit them to proceed economically. That has not been possible in the past. As a result of the policy of this government the Mackenzie highway has been completed, hand in hand with the proposal to construct this railway, and I am sure the Northwest Territories and the general vicinity of the north will benefit tremendously.
Apart from the question of economics, and I think I have said sufficient to indicate that there is vast promise there and great benefits which will inevitably result from the completion of this railroad, there is a sociological factor which cannot be ignored. I have touched upon the first aspect of that already. For many, many years promises have been made and broken but we now have a government which has kept its pledge to the people. I suggest that fact will have a great effect on the minds of the people, particularly those thousands who went into that north country with the firm understanding that a railroad would be constructed. Those individuals have hewn out their farmland from the forest, have trucked their supplies in and hauled their grain out over 250 miles at a cost of 40 cents a bushel. These people have persisted in the face of these difficulties, and now at last they have a government which keeps its word.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the completion of this railroad will provide opportunities for the small people. The days of the pioneer, as I saw them when I first went into the Peace river country, have to a large extent diminished. There will be made available in those areas opened up by the construction of this railroad hundreds of thousands of opportunities for individuals who wish to establish themselves, employ themselves in carving out new carers, new lives, and new homes. It is my firm belief that there will develop shortly on this continent a substantial trek into areas such as this of those individuals who feel that some of the large and more ungainly centres of civilization do not offer what they seek.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, if I may be allowed to use a phrase which was used by a great British statesman many years ago, I think the Prime Minister and members of this government by this measure have called into being a new land in part to redress the balance of the old.

I think it might be said, however, that will provide some bread and butter at this time.

speechtext:
I will attempt to show you that is exactly what I am doing at the moment, to a far greater extent than anyone in the C.C.F. party will do.
I spoke in regard to this matter when I first was elected to this house during my maiden speech as it appears in Hansard of May 19, 1958. I advocated the building of this railroad using the route that is now being adopted by the present government. At that same time the hon. member for Peace River took a very active part and undoubtedly deserves much credit for the fact that this route has been chosen because he brought out facts to show that this was the proper route, and also did a great deal of work in this regard during the Manning commission. I am sure that the people of the

Peace River area both in Alberta and British Columbia owe much to the hon. member for Peace River.
After I had spoken in regard to this matter in my maiden speech in this house I received a letter from the premier of the province of British Columbia who, after having congratulated me, in respect to my maiden speech, made the following statement as it appears in that letter:
I was gratified that in this first speech that you dealt with the development of northern British Columbia and Alberta and wish to thank you especially for the remarks which you made regarding the building of a railroad from Pine Point in the Northwest Territories. I presume you had in mind that the road would go to the neighbourhood of Grimshaw, a point on the northern Alberta railway which is owned jointly by the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways. The traffic would then have a choice either to go by the N.A.R. to Edmonton or by the N.A.R. west to connect with the Pacific Great Eastern Railway at the British Columbia border. Along with this point of view, our bureau of economics has been carrying out some research and for your information I am enclosing their preliminary report. If you are interested, I will be glad to send you any further information we are able to get.
This letter was signed by W. A. C. Bennett, premier of the province of British Columbia. I hope that full use is going to be made of this railway, and that we will see a good deal of traffic going over the Pacific Great Eastern Railway lines because I believe it will be of great benefit both to the Peace river area of British Columbia and of Alberta.
The government of the province of British Columbia took a very active part in trying to provide information with respect to the route which should be chosen for this railroad. I should just like to read two statements from the brief which they submitted to the royal commission on the Great Slave lake railway. They are on page 3 of their brief and read as follows:
The purpose of this government in making the present submission is twofold:
(a)	In the national interest, it is felt that the proposed rail extension constitutes an important and necessary initial step in the development of the resources of the Mackenzie district and will make a major contribution to the expansion, growth, and development of northern Canada.
Of course, this quite clearly bears out the view many of the members have expressed, namely that this ties in very closely with the whole northern development policy of the present government. After the many years of delay and talk about this railway it is most encouraging to see that action is going to be taken by the present administration.
The second paragraph in the brief reads as follows:
(b)	As a partner with the province of Alberta in responsibility for the geographical region known as the Peace ri ,'er district, which lies partly within

British Columbia boundaries, this province wishes to make available its special knowledge of the said area in view of the fact that two of three proposed railway routes run through the Peace river district.
Of course, they went on to advocate the western route which has now been chosen by the government. Regardless of what the hon. member for Kootenay West might think, I believe I am speaking for the people of British Columbia when I say I wish to congratulate the government on having chosen the proper route, based on all the facts as they were put before the royal commission. The government deserves commendation in that after the long delay of many years and promises made by former governments this government is taking action to speed up the development of Canada.
