speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the day that I have waited for ever since I came to this house. Unfortunately, perhaps, for some of the residents of my district the railroad is going through the Peace river district. I spoke strongly for the railroad going through my part of the country naturally because the eastern half of northern Alberta is equally rich in resources as the western half. Nevertheless water transport is the life blood of the eastern half of northern Alberta and I have always seen the orderly development of the north country tied in with roads and water transport. Although a railroad is essential for the orderly development of the north country, I have always stressed on our side the need for adequate highways and better water transport. Unfortunately, again the question of building roads in eastern Alberta is largely the responsibility of the provincial government. Our far seeing government has developed a tremendous program of roads to resources. This is the only hope I have of getting superior and rapid development of roads in northeastern Alberta, and I have concentrated most of my efforts in this direction.
Kind remarks were made about me by the hon. member for Peace River and my respect for the hon. member is equal to that of any hon. member in this house because he also has taken a very impartial view. He has demanded that all the facts be put on the table. I do not know whether all the facts have been put on the table yet, but we appointed a royal commission to look into this matter. I have read its reports very carefully and I think it made a fair decision in this case.
I should like to have sat on a commission myself, not as a member of a royal commission but on a fact-finding board. Had I been appointed to such a board, then it would have
Canadian National Railways been said about the decision that I had played petty party politics and regional politics. In a situation of this kind the appointment of a royal commission was the only fair way to make an impartial decision, or certainly one which would be accepted by the people of Canada as such.
The accusation that this road is being built purely as window dressing is far from the truth. This is an essential part of what we are still proud to call the vision, the development of northern Canada. If we wait until we have orders from mining companies, timber companies or any other kind of companies before we build a railroad we may never get those companies into the north country. Railroads are essentially a pioneer project. When Sir John A. Macdonald signed the final order to build the C.P.R. this was vision, a vision which made Canada what she is today, and this move of the government to build this great railway into the north as fast as possible and as far as possible, I predict will have the same kind of result.
The great development of the north country cannot help but benefit not only northwestern Alberta but northeastern Alberta, the whole of Alberta and the whole of our country. The pioneering spirit is not dead in Canada, and this I think will give it that shot in the arm which is needed at this particular time.
Lead and zinc are on the south shore of Great Slave lake, one of the richest deposits on the planet. I do not know how soon we are going to need those deposits, but I understand that at the present time we are in short supply. I am for any company, be it the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, or any other company which takes a forward view and wants Canada to be well stocked with all the munitions of war and peace.
I am one of those who still believe that the leadership given by privately owned and operated corporations is the finest way of raising the standard of living in Canada, in North America, yes, in the whole world. I think it is an unfair thing to say that we are building this railroad for any company because the railroad serves us all. That is why we pay deficits. I say we will not pay deficits if we build those railroads to the right places and carry them to the right places to develop the resources of our country. I say build it now.
I want to pay tribute to the hon. member for Mackenzie River who is not here today. I am sure he would be glad to be here to see one of his dreams come true, because he is a man who sees the development of Canada as a whole. He puts party politics to one side. I remember seeing him standing in this house some time ago, and I remember

Canadian National Railways hearing him say, "I don't care where you build it; I just want to know that you will build it as soon as possible."
There have been so-called delays but those delays have been occasioned so that we could build it the best way, the cheapest way, the most efficient way and the way that will serve the whole of Canada, including British Columbia, in the most efficient manner.
There is another reason for building this railroad into the north country, and that is it will help us develop the southern part of our country as well. I can see the day when this railroad to the north from Grimshaw into the Great Slave country will be linked with a line running to the east into Saskatchewan and through my district. One or two very short links would connect the lines of Canadian National Railways north of the Saskatchewan river and provide an efficient railway service to the whole of the parkland stretching from Edmonton to Prince Albert.
Railroads do not only serve mining and agriculture. They are also very important for defence purposes. The proper linking of railways today is all-important when such things as Bomarcs and other rocket equipment will be needed if and when we have a war. In defending North America our defence will have to be extremely mobile, and I look to the day when we will have a network of railways and not the kind of bottlenecks that we have today.
In order to travel into northern Alberta today by railroad you have to go through the city of Edmonton. All the railroad lines fan out of Edmonton. We live in the atomic age and one atomic bomb on Edmonton would paralyse all the railroads in northern Alberta. If our railroads are going to operate efficiently both in war and peace it is essential that we have a proper, sensible network and eliminate these bottlenecks.
So I look to the day when lines of Canadian National Railways in northern Saskatchewan and northern Alberta are linked together, and it would not take very many miles of railway line to do this. In one place the gap is only 40 miles and this would eliminate an additional haul of 328 miles from Frenchman Butte in Saskatchewan to Heinsburg which is just east of the flourishing town of St. Paul. If this link were closed we would have a short cut between Winnipeg and Cold Lake airport which is today a most important part of the air defence of North America.
Railroading is not dead; it is simply inefficient at the present time. I have said before in the house that I am not a railroader, but if you will take a look at the railroad map of northern Alberta you will see two things. First of all, you will see that we need a link with the Northwest Territories, which

we are going to build, and, second, we need to link this great north and south railroad with a line east and west so that we can cut down extra mileage in freight hauls and can have a network for the defence of the whole of northwestern Canada which is of great importance today.
I believe in the future of railroading because we are a pioneer country and we will be hauling heavy freight which can be handled most efficiently by railroads. Perhaps this railroad will not pay for itself in one year but over a period of 50 years it will apy off a thousandfold. It will develop Canada in depth.
It has been said that we are only building this railroad because of the mineral resources. This is not true. The hon. member for Peace River has shown that the potential in timber with proper modern timber farming methods means that northern Alberta will be a very rich source of both timber and pulp once we have rail facilities into that country. I need not stress the importance of the tar sands. In my district alone there are between 200 billion and 500 billion barrels of tar and oil-producing tar sands. Having in mind the situation in Kuwait which may blow up at any time, we can realize the importance of this resource because we may need the oil. I say that we need vision and we should take steps to encourage private companies to go there and develop that great national resource.
Great Slave lake and all the other lakes of the north are rich in fish and fishing is essential to the incomes of our metis and Indian populations. The supply has only been scratched. We can bring tons and tons of fish from the north country by rail and this will be of tremendous help to the Indians and metis in the northern part of my riding in assisting them to earn a living by working at something to which they are eminently fitted. This has been a traditional way of life with the metis and the Indians who take to fishing particularly as a natural way of earning their living. We can show no better faith than by helping them to develop the fishing industry over the period of the next 25 years.
There are also large deposits of gypsum which is very important today. The supply of gypsum is almost unlimited. Iron ore has now been found in northern Alberta. The Northern Alberta Railroad is one railroad which has been paying its way. I think this is very important at the present time when some of the other railroads are experiencing such large deficits. Some people say that we should not build any more railroads but we should certainly build them where they will make money. One reason they are making money lies in the fact that their freight rates for transporting cargo into the north are

exorbitant. This is another reason why I should like to see railroads and roads into the north built at the same time because in that way we would have competition.
When I speak of private enterprise may I say that I am not one who believes in monopoly. This is one reason why I have suggested that when this railway into the north has been constructed there would be nothing wrong with building a second railroad into the north. One could run through the Peace river district and the other could run from Fort McMurray to the south shore of Great Slave lake. At the present time this might look like duplication but I think it will not be very many years before the railroad into the north which we are going to construct will be so busy that we will need two lines. Instead of constructing a double track route at that time I think we should have one line running through the Peace river district and one running north from Fort McMurray.
I think any fair-minded person who reads the report of the royal commission will say that the need is greater at the present moment on the western route. Anybody who cannot see that the north country will support two railways and that the future of the north country is almost unlimited lacks vision. A lack of vision cannot be attributed to the present government because they have vision and are doing something about these things.
Before I came to Ottawa I made an election promise that I would do all I could to promote the building of railroads both north and south and east and west where they are required and I say that such lines will make money. Let us be realistic. Let us have no socialist snow poured upon the sunny Alberta scene. If the socialists do not have any positive suggestions to make, let them sit on the sidelines and watch how a dynamic, selfreliant free enterprise system really works. We need every citizen in Canada behind this project. Do not look to the old party with the new face. Just open your eyes and see what the old party with the same old vision, the same old hope and the same old faith does when you put them in power and give them a chance to do so. We have been given this chance and we are taking advantage of it. We do not think such projects are a sad gamble.
I believe in the future of this country in the same way that my grandparents did, and they pioneered in this great district of northern Alberta in the early 1800's. Hon. members will excuse me if I tell them that my grandfather was the Hudson Bay factor at Lac La Biche, which is the territorial centre of my district, from 1874 to 1881. My mother would have been born there but there was
Canadian National Railways only one white man in the whole country, my grandfather, and he took his wife to Fort Pitt in Saskatchewan so my maternal ancestor's home was in that fair province of Saskatchewan. It is for this reason I am interested in the development of road and rail facilities in northern Saskatchewan. This is another part of the country that is going to benefit from railroads and roads built as a result of this government's vision.
How can you say on the one hand that we have had delay and, on the other hand, say that we are building it too fast? We do not believe this is the case. We believe we have delayed only the necessary time for investigating all the facts. I myself asked to have these facts investigated. I compliment this government upon carrying out this investigation not hastily but thoroughly. I do not believe we will have to apologize for the results. By 1967, the 100th anniversary of our country, I am sure the results of this project will be evident. I do not believe there will be any more delay. The survey parties are on the ground and are already providing employment. Pretty soon we will be cutting the rights of way and we will be keeping the promises made by former governments over the last 30 years. We accept responsibility for promises made by the federal government, and we carry them out in the same manner as we carried out the promise to build the Saskatchewan dam.
Great credit has been given to former ministers of agriculture and other prime ministers for their vision in respect of these projects, but it has taken this government to put them into action. One should recall that this has been done at a time when world conditions have made trade a difficult thing, when we have had to get out there and sell like we never did before. We are recovering our markets, and it is these markets that will keep our railroads busy. It was not long ago that we said we had too much wheat. Today it looks as though we are not going to have enough. When father sun smiles too brightly on the prairies, our surpluses dwindle. Now we are selling all the wheat we can grow and we are going to keep growing it, we are going to keep selling it and it will take the railroads to haul it.
The last time we had a serious drought on the prairies thousands of people flocked into the Peace river country. They were promised a railroad to enable them to sell their agricultural products. It is a sad thing that they have had to wait so long to see the fulfilment of this promise. I, for one, am very pleased that they are getting the railroad. I look forward to the day when branch lines from this railroad will serve the whole of the

Canadian National Railways north country, thus lowering the cost ol transporting freight and serving the people on my side of Alberta. This is the kind of service for which they have been looking for the last 30 years. The town of McMurray is dependent on water transport. I do not believe the town of McMurray is going to suffer at all from the building of the railway. When the north is developed the way it should be we will be loading our barges with more freight because the railroads will have helped to develop the north country. Water transport is the cheapest form of transport, and as long as water transport facilities are serviced by adequate roads north out of Edmonton to McMurray, then water transport will be able to compete. It is competition that develops, not monopoly. I do not worry about the railroads having competition because there is going to be lots of work for everybody. The railroads will be busy and the roads will be busy.
At the moment, the airways are carrying the passenger traffic. I have spoken to air line officials as recently as yesterday and they are happy that this railroad is to be constructed because they know that the development of the north will mean increased business for them. They will give fast service to the passengers and the light freight, but they know that only roads and railroads can develop the northern part of the country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words today in commendation of the hon. member for Peace River. I believe he has every reason to feel proud and gratified in the knowledge that his many hard years of work on behalf of this railway have finally borne fruit in the form of this resolution. In order that hon. members will properly understand what the railway means to northern Alberta and the Northwest Territories, perhaps I should say a few words about the geography of that part of the country.
I am sure that not all hon. members realize that we are not just west but are considerably north of this part of Ontario. If we were to project the city of Ottawa in a direct westerly line, Ottawa would be in the southern part of the state of Montana. Edmonton is nearly in the middle of the province of Alberta, and the rest of the province is so undeveloped that it is equivalent to parts of northern Ontario. I should say that those parts of northern Ontario about which you are used to thinking of forests, streams, hunting and fishing, are about on the same latitude as Edmonton. North of Edmonton we soon find a forest area. There is almost a solid forest area north and west of Edmonton right to the mountains. The solid forest extends north to the tundra regions.

There is only one real exception to this, and that is the Peace river country which occupies part of northern Alberta and part of British Columbia. This is extremely fertile farm land and very beautiful country. The temperatures are about the same as they are in the rest of Alberta and the normal rainfall is conducive to raising good crops. There has been such an increase in the population of the area that more and more farm land suitable for agriculture is being developed. The Peace river country extends quite a distance in an easterly and westerly direction and finds an outlet for its products to the west in British Columbia through Prince George and down to Vancouver or through Edmonton. There is a narrow strip of land along the Mackenzie highway north of the Peace river itself which is being developed as farm land.
In looking at the development of this part of the country while travelling through it on the highway we get some idea of the reason for the construction of this railway. The farm lands in the north are scattered and there are few settlements which are now as close to the highway as they can get, so they are making use of a very narrow, thin strip of the agricultural land that is available. The problem of importing the things they need and exporting their produce is extremely difficult. I have not ridden through that country in a vehicle for quite a few years, but I have watched the statistics and I know that for all practical purposes development of agricultural lands north of Manning, Alberta, has practically ceased; there is very little expansion.
That territory is capable of providing good farm land for many, many times the present population. There is very good land there. When we see the House of Commons and the government of this country giving consideration to the necessity for taking uneconomic land out of cultivation, of shifting the land from a use which was not intended, back into pasturage, etc., it becomes very apparent why it is such a shame to have what is some of the finest land in the country laying barren, unused because of transportation difficulties.
Those who suggest that the only use of this railway is to haul ore really have not given the geography of the northern part of Alberta much consideration. It is a very significant fact, I think, that the railway is going to carry on from the end of the N.A.R. which is already established in the territory. The N.A.R. railway goes to Peace River by a somewhat circuitous route. The trip is fairly long. It is twice as long by rail to Peace River as it is by road; it is twice as long in miles and it is twice as long in time. The

significance of this is that it is extremely unlikely, therefore, that this railroad will be called upon to provide any passenger service to any great extent.
I am not an expert on railways, but I have heard a good deal of emphasis placed on the losses incurred by passenger traffic on the railways. It does seem that railways are always attempting to curtail passenger services to various points and the residents of those points are usually objecting most strenuously. I think that to begin with there will not be the demand for passengers to that part of the country because the country right now is quite sparsely settled. There will not likely be the demand for that service in the future because there is a much shorter road connection, and when you are taking journeys further than from Peace River to Edmonton aircraft is now the accepted mode of transportation. In view of this fact I do not think there will be the heavy drain on railroad revenues with which other lines have to contend.
Next there is the fact that the mine potential of Pine Point is really very, very huge. There is no doubt that the amount of ore to be hauled out of that territory will mean that the railway will be able to operate in the most efficient manner possible. I understand that the soundest financial business for a railway to be in is the long haul of full trainloads on a non-stop basis. Therefore they have here the full potential for economic operation. They will be able to load and assemble full trainloads at a time; they will be able to move these trainloads long distances without many of the normal traffic hazards, without the necessity for frequent stops, etc. The produce of the mines to be developed at Pine Point should be a sufficient guarantee that this railway will be a paying proposition.
Of course, the people of that area are not just interested in the fact that a railroad is going through or that there is going to be a big development at Pine Point. The constituents of the Peace River district are interested in the railway because they see themselves being able to obtain some benefits out of it. That railway will certainly haul the wheat, the cattle and the supplies into that country for those people.
I imagine that it will be only a very short time before the farming population in the area north of Grimshaw will be doubled, and then doubled again. There is room for these people. There is splendid land there. With a good railway operating efficiently, which can therefore give economical rates, there will be plenty of opportunity for the northern farmers to compete with the farmers in the
Canadian National Railways rest of the province and in the other provinces. It is only the high cost of transportation which has caused these valuable lands to be considered not valuable today because of their remoteness. I predict that their full value will start to be known and they will start to be developed within a very few years.
While the commission was considering the route for this railroad a great deal of agitation was being carried on by various groups and organizations who were trying to influence the government to go one way or the other. Many of the arguments used were, I thought, a little specious. Some I thought were merely advanced in an attempt to scare, because some people had private motives which were not at all those which they enunciated to the public.
I do recall, for instance, that in the city of Edmonton some people were trying to get the city to throw its full weight behind the eastern route, the route from Fort McMurray, because they said, "This business will all go to Vancouver. The trains will all move out through British Columbia. This traffic will not go through Edmonton and we will lose it".
I think the people who advanced those arguments were doing the city of Edmonton a great disservice. I do not believe for one minute that the majority of the citizens of Edmonton would insist on the railway going the eastern route merely because it might be better for them, without any consideration to which route would be in the best interests of the people in the north and in the rest of Canada. I cannot understand how so many people in Edmonton could have been panicked by this sort of talk. Surely a city like Edmonton, which has been known as the gateway to the north for many, many years, realizes the importance of Edmonton as a supply centre. Surely the people of Edmonton realize the impact on that city that occurred every time any part of the north was opened up. Demands for goods and services increase as the population increases. The capacity of those people to buy Edmonton's goods and services increases as the north part of the country increases in wealth.
I think the first result is going to be a greatly increased population growth in the north. The effects will be felt in northern Alberta first, and then all the way north. Edmonton, as a supply centre, cannot help but benefit by reason of that increase. There may well be a certain diversion of traffic through to the Pacific coast, but no one, I think, is going to suggest for a moment that traffic should not go where it is most convenient and where it can be most efficiently handled. But I suggest that the

Canadian National Railways amount diverted will be only a small part of the increased potential which the city of Edmonton will find in that new bigger and richer north which this railway will make possible.
I am not saying, of course, that merely put-ing a railroad in there is automatically going to make anyone rich. Everyone who contemplates a new venture should remember that a railway is not a source of wealth in itself. A railway, like any other means of transportation, represents merely a drain on resources -a factor to be overcome, in the same way as road transport is. Transportation is a cost which has to be borne by every business. We do have the opportunity, however, of getting the minerals out of Pine Point and we should talk of the railway as being that vehicle which seems to have potential as a means of reducing the costs which we have been facing up to this time.
I can recall the misleading pictures which some people have painted about this. There was in Edmonton at one time a newspaper called the Edmonton Bullet, and I still remember the flaming red headline three or four inches high which appeared one day calling attention to a tremendous lead discovery. This was merely going to prove the greatest find of wealth in years and years and they gave the discovery great headlines on a full front page. However, on reading the article it became obvious that these dreams were not to be realized. The lead was lining the Arctic ocean along the extreme northern coast of Canada. Brief reflection showed that it would cost twice as much to move the lead out of there to a civilized part of Canada as the lead was worth. I am merely telling the story to illustrate that wealth is not all it appears on the surface and that these costs, particularly the costs of transportation, are very real things with which to contend.
I know that some people have not paid enough attention to the means of transportation at their disposal. Some people have not made the best use of the transportation which was available. There is, for instance, not very much general knowledge of the size of the fishing industry on the Great Slave lake. I understand that about ten million pounds of fish a year are taken out of that lake. That is a lot of fish when one considers that the product has to be moved 800 miles over a highway to get to Edmonton. It has to be flown a long distance if it is taken out by plane. I believe the construction of a railway will have a great effect on the cost of transporting this fish. Obviously if we had been able to develop an industry which takes approximately 10 million pounds of fish capable of being sold through our present inadequate


type of transport the potential must be considerably larger if we could overcome part of the cost of transportation. I am sure we shall see new canneries being built in Hay River, perhaps in Yellowknife and perhaps towards the east end of Great Slave lake.
The size of this lake is generally not understood in other parts of the country. It ranks just next to Great Bear lake in area, and Great Bear lake and Great Slave lake are both larger than lake Erie.

It should therefore be possible for us to have large quantities of freight which can be moved in train loads or, at least, in car lots. There will certainly be trainloads of ore. There will be car lots of timber and

fish, car lots, and probably train loads, of grain, cattle and so on. All of this is what the railway calls paying business. All of this makes it possible for a railway to make good money. I am emphasizing this because in my discussions with people in Edmonton about the railway I found that in general the citizens had become alarmed at the thought of a new railway because they had heard so much about railroads losing money, about railroads wanting to discontinue services to certain points and similar troubles. They think of the present age as an air age, an age of competition from trucks and so on. They were growing concerned about investing the sums of money necessary to build another railroad.
I think it should be said that this type of railroading is still a good business investment. This type of railroading will still compete with any type of transportation in the country and it will still make the business a paying proposition.
I should like to say a few words about the members of the Manning commission. I know they have worked extremely hard on this task, and I think the government's choice of the membership of the commission was excellent. Mr. Ted Manning is a lawyer who has lived in Edmonton almost all his life. He has had many dealings with the north of Alberta and the Northwest Territories in the course of his practice. He has travelled all over the region and has an extensive first hand knowledge of the country and its problems. Mr. John Anderson Thompson, the other member of the commission, comes from Yellowknife where he has been in business for many years. He has an extensive knowledge of the problems of the north, especially transportation. Nobody could live in Yellowknife for many years and carry on a construction business there without understanding fully the importance of cheaper transportation. Mr. Gainer gave to the committee, I thought, balance. He brought, perhaps, a more scholastic view to its deliberations. He was perhaps not as directly involved with some of the decisions and could, therefore, give a more detached view of the proceedings.
Mr. Chairman, I hope I have not exhausted the patience of the members of this committee. Mr. Chairman, quite frankly I may be a little out of my usual form. Being a green member here I usually speak once a year, and by speaking now have placed myself out of that category. However, this bill regarding the construction of that railroad line in northern Alberta is a subject of such importance that I feel I must call attention to several facts and compliment those who have been responsible for bringing this bill before this committee. I should like to outline several reasons why hon. members should support this resolution in order to get the project into production.
The first time I heard about this railroad was during the 1958 campaign. Being a farmer from the opposite end of Alberta I was not too much interested in it. In rising this afternoon I recall particular things concerning the development of northern Canada. If my memory serves me correctly many statements have been made about visions. One statement contained words which are clearer to me today, having been in this house for four years, than they were when I first heard them. Those words were "a vision from igloo to igloo".
When I first heard those words as a new campaigner in the federal field I was actually disturbed and quite frankly had a difficult time understanding their meaning. Those words have particular meaning for me today when considered in conjunction with certain pertinent facts concerning our natural resources, and particularly those of lead and zinc. How much longer will Canada be able to supply her own needs for lead and zinc without the further development represented by the bill now before this committee? I

Canadian National Railways have heard from reliable sources that if this railway is not developed very shortly enabling this ore to reach our smelters we will have to import such ore.

speechtext:
Yes, I am quite aware of that. However, as I said earlier I am talking about the situation in Canada as a nation.
I suggest that Canada is in great danger of facing the necessity of importing certain resources which exist in Canada in great quantities. I suggest that we are in danger of this, and suggest it quite emphatically. I am speaking of the nation as a whole. In light of certain facts, views and ideas which have been

expressed in this committee over the last few years I have come to realize that certain people would not be unhappy with increased importation of certain natural resources because they advocate high tariffs. I take no issue with that view but only suggest that certain people would like to see this come about.
As an Albertan, a Canadian and a Conservative I am very proud to be able to speak in regard to this proposal because I feel that our natural resources should be developed to the greatest extent possible. I do only refer to mineral resources but, as a farmer, I refer to agricultural products as well. I am particularly interested in agriculture and should like to take a moment or two of the committee's valuable time to say a word or two in this regard.
I have listened quite patiently very often to much discussion about overproduction and surpluses of agricultural products. We have heard this all through the agricultural debates. I think we have an example before us today, Mr. Chairman, which makes us realize that a great deal of the discussion was idle talk. We have literally millions of acres available adjacent to the area that this railway will serve. To those who say that we should not open up new agricultural areas, that we would thereby contribute to our surpluses and to our present difficulties I would simply point out in discussing this matter that it is not a fact. You can take the one burning issue that so many people have had so much to say about in this house and across the country, namely the wheat surplus, and you will see today that certain facts have borne out certain ideas that we on this side of the house have been trying to put forward for some time. Our surplus, if you wish to call it that, is certainly not what some members have tried to say it was.
It can be looked at in this way. There are many businessmen in this house. Let us take any product, I do not care whether it is wheat, apples, strawberries, lead, zinc, or what have you. If you are in the business of selling that product, and particularly if you are in a highly competitive business, you know that when a customer comes to you and you cannot supply the article he wants you will say, "I am sorry, I have not that article in stock but if you would not mind coming back next week I will have it for you". Well, in this day and age, with a highly competitive product and in a highly competitive market that customer will not come back.
I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that if we are in that business, certainly it does not behoove us to talk about surpluses. I have listened patiently to this talk for several years since I have been in the house. I would

remind certain hon. members opposite that today we can see where our surplus is. There are agricultural experts opposite. I ask, where is the surplus? To hark back to my analogy; actually do we have a complete stock deal? Are all the articles on the shelf? For the information of hon. members I should like to say I am very happy also to know that the government has already taken steps to alleviate that lack of what I call stock. Therefore, in considering this railroad, Mr. Chairman, and the various aspects of it, such as mineral production and agriculture in particular, we must consider every angle we possibly can. I am only trying to point out some of the things that I am very happy to consider.
Another thing has been pointed out very well previously by several hon. members who spoke on this resolution that we all support regardless of party. I have heard no one say that he did not support it today. There was a great deal of criticism-I think it was constructive criticism-about the time spent studying where the location of the road should be. There was a great deal of discussion on the economics of the road. We are all interested in economics, and particularly in the cost of such a thing as a railroad. But there was one point that probably some of us failed to consider. I refer to the things that were to be hauled by this railroad from its most southerly point. The tonnages were heavy. The tonnage that will be hauled over the railroad has been referred to quite well by other hon. members; but the point I wish to make is that railroads today are different from those of 20 years ago, or even 10 years ago. The road beds are almost unrecognizable, comparatively speaking, because they have to be built in such a way so far as ballasting and grades are concerned that railroaders did not consider years ago. The only point I am trying to make is that in the studies by the commission and by all interested parties, it was apparent that the eastern route might be the most economical or the cheaper route to take simply because it costs less money to build a railroad from the end of the Northern Alberta Railroad by way of the east route to Pine Point where they intended to go. I would go along with that, Mr. Chairman, actually.
One point was left out. I never heard it mentioned by anyone vitally concerned with this railroad. It is simply this. When the railroad reached that southerly point it then had to go several hundred miles over the old roadbed of the N.A.R. Even the N.A.R. today has trouble in face of the drought and other problems affecting western Canada. There are portions of the present N.A.R. on the eastern side that cannot supply adequate facilities, for the equipment that is travelling 90205-6-1634
Canadian National Railways over that railroad today. If I may say so, the equipment is old, proportionately weak and light. The passenger train that goes there today was retired from service on the C.P.R. in 1927.
When this railway is complete it will be equipped with diesel locomotives which will take long strings of larger cars; perhaps twice or three times as long, I am really not too sure. The loads and the speeds will be greater. The present railroad has trouble. They may have to drag a train up out of the muskeg. It happens almost daily. They have a schedule but no one really knows when any freight train or even a light passenger train will arrive at its destination. In view of that I ask hon. members, is there any argument about the most feasible route being the western route?
I have taken some time, Mr. Chairman and I know that hon. members on the other side and probably other hon. members may think I have taken too much time. We have been talking about facts, figures and economics but I have heard no one say very much about the people that this railway line will serve. Comparatively speaking, there are a great many people living along the western route and very few living along the eastern route. While it is our duty to consider to the best of our ability all the economic factors, and I think we have, I certainly do not think that as elected representatives of the people we should completely ignore the personal factor.
I live almost at the other end of the province of Alberta but I know people from that portion of the province and have visited some of them. Neighbours of mine have gone to that area of Alberta and are farming there. I know the problems that they have. In view of the fact that there may have been some controversy and argument as to the route that should be followed-I hope there is none at this stage-certainly the personal factor should be given at least equal status with economic considerations. I am happy to be able to say these few words in support of of this project in spite of the fact that the hon. member for Trinity thinks we are taking an unwarranted amount of time, and in spite of all the emphasis on facts and figures I want to leave the thought with hon. members that we must consider the personal element.
The boon to the people can well be imagined. Whether or not there is going to be passenger service there will be a train going up and down the line probably every day or possibly several trains a day. I do not know what the schedule will be. However, it is quite a satisfaction to a backwoodsman in such an area to know that there will be a train going by his door or through his

Canadian National Railways community and that if he is in trouble or needs certain services those services and that assistance will be available to him.

Mr. Chairman, I could not let this occasion pass without saying a few words in support of the resolution. For some considerable time prior to my entry into public life I supported the principle involved in the construction of this railroad and once I had come to parliament I assisted the hon. member for Peace River and others from the province of Alberta and western Canada generally in convincing the government that we should proceed with the building of the line.
There was some effort on the part of the official opposition to take credit for the idea and its ultimate fruition in the decision to go ahead with this railway. I should like to say, as was indicated quite adequately by the hon. member for Peace River, that this railroad had been a promise that had been dangled before the eyes of the people of the Peace River bloc for a quarter of a century or more but under the present government something was actually done about it.
I recall quite well the history of the Pine Point railroad in the last few years. It was first indicated during the election campaign of 1958 that the government was going to go ahead with this project and in the first speech from the throne thereafter there was an indication that the government was proceeding with the plan.
I would point out to hon. gentlemen opposite, whose knowledge of this area is cursory, that quite a case can be made to support either of the two points of view with respect to where this railroad should go. However, a commission of inquiry was appointed which heard both sides of the question and also served to dispel some rather illusory knowledge and to eradicate from certain circles in Ottawa ideas about the potentialities, conditions and characteristics of the area. May I say that I have travelled through both areas, although I did so some years ago, and have some rough idea as to potential costs.
The commission of inquiry was appointed in 1959 and turned in its report in June of 1960. In line with the majority report the government indicated in the speech from the throne in the fall of 1960 that it would proceed with the construction of the railroad along a particular route. I cannot see how it can be said that there was any undue delay. Any time anyone talks about delay they seem to be critical. I am not limiting my criticism to remarks made by the opposition in chiding the government with delay but am also referring as well to certain newspapers which have taken the government to task. I think


they have done so without a true appreciation of all the facts involved. Such a project does not materialize out of thin air. We all know that there had to be a great deal of negotiation between the government, the railroads and the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company in order to arrive at some plan to finance this program of railroad construction.
The hon. member for Kootenay West requested that this matter should be referred to a committee and that all sorts of people should be called before that committee to satisfy members of the house that various conditions have been met. I would simply refer him to the proceedings of the Manning commission of inquiry. Representatives of the type referred to by the hon. member appeared there, and many more. If the hon. member would take the trouble to read the report, if he would take the trouble to read the submission of the government of the province of British Columbia, he would not make such a request. After all, the government of British Columbia made quite a play so far as this railroad is concerned, and I want to talk about that a little later.
The hon. member believes we should undertake this inquiry. However, when the railroads were built into Chibougamau and Thompson lake, this house was asked to approve expenditures by Canadian National Railways to undertake the construction of these lines. No such request was made by the hon. member for Kootenay West or anyone else to have certain people give this information. With the greatest respect, I would suggest the hon. member should gather together the material that was submitted to the Manning commission which conducted the inquiry into the construction of this railroad.
I feel that this is the first step toward the development of the Northwest Territories. In my opinion Hay River, which is to be developed into a lake port on the south shore of Great Slave lake, is the natural jumping off point for the Northwest Territories. Hay River is served by the Mackenzie highway which gives access from Grimshaw and then goes around the Mackenzie river to Yellowknife. This is the jumping off place for the development of that vast trench of the Mackenzie river all the way down to the Arctic coast. It is true that the development will lessen as one goes farther north. Having spent some time travelling up and down the Mackenzie river as far north as Norman Wells, I have gained a true appreciation of the vast potential that lies in this central trunk of communications.
In so far as this area of northwestern Alberta is concerned-and the same considerations apply to the northeastern part

Aeronautics Act
of British Columbia-I may say that the area has been within the economic ambit of Edmonton. It is for that reason I am speaking on this measure this afternoon. I know that as a member of the Edmonton chamber of commerce I found it difficult to support the chamber's contention that the route of the railway should be the eastern route through Waterways, Alberta. The chamber has known all along that I did not approve of this support. It is a judgment decision and the factors are not 100 per cent one way or 100 per cent the other way. On balance, however, I was of the opinion that the proper route was the western route.
I would repeat that the whole of the Peace river country and the Northwest Territories has lain within the economic ambit of Edmonton. However, the British Columbia government has built the P.G.E. as far as Dawson Creek. I believe it now behooves businessmen and organizations in Edmonton and in northern Alberta to look to their laurels. This area, with its vast potential, cannot be considered to lie easily within the grasp of business concerns and organizations in Alberta. I think, myself, that it would be likely that most of the railroad business that will be developed by this line will be the transportation of ore through Edmonton, to Calgary and out to Trail because that is the easiest and cheapest route. I believe, too, that supplies coming in from eastern Canada and from the manufacturing area of Edmonton and Calgary, will move over this line rather than come over the P.G.E. from Vancouver. However, I feel that competition will be good. It will keep our people in Edmonton on their toes. Certainly, the highway connections between Edmonton and Great Slave lake are far superior to any existing in British Columbia.
Now, in so far as the construction of the line is concerned, may I make a suggestion to the minister. I suggest that rather than make this a "do it yourself" proposition using the consulting engineers and the resources of the railroad, local firms in Alberta and British Columbia should be used. After all, there is a problem of time involved here. It is said the construction will take four years. We know that Consolidated Mining and Smelting is worried about their source of raw materials for the next two or three years. They would like the construction of this railroad expedited as much as possible. If the railway has not got facilities to expedite construction, then they should use outside firms.
For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I felt that I had to say something about this resolution, and I would commend it to the members of this committee.

Amendment agreed to.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
