speechtext: It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of public and private bills, the former having precedence.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-37, to amend the Aeronautics Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak on Bill No. C-37, I feel it is one of the most important enactments to be brought before the house in the form of a private member's bill. It may appear at first blush, on looking at the actual wording of the bill, that it is exceptionally complex, but I hope in the brief time at my disposal to strip some of the complexities from the bill and indicate very clearly what I think are the most important principles facing the house at this particular time.
Briefly, the objective of this bill is to establish a central aircraft registry, probably in the city of Ottawa, to record title to and charges against Canadian civil aircraft, aircraft engines, propellers and spare parts. Many hon. members are no doubt familiar with the central type of registry covering motor vehicles that we find in many of the provinces. Hon. members from provinces such as British Columbia which operate under the Torrens system of land registry will also be familiar with the central type of land registry. Similarly, the objective of this bill is to apply the concept of a central type of registry to civil aircraft.
What are the reasons for doing this? First of all, when an individual is acquiring an aircraft which may cost $10,000 or more I think the most important thing is that he should be able to obtain clear title to that aircraft. The aircraft has an even greater degree of mobility than is involved in ownership of motor vehicles and, of course, we have a central registry covering motor vehicles.
The difficulty facing any purchaser acquiring an aircraft is first of all to find out where that aircraft has been. It is possible, naturally, for the aircraft to cover almost all the provinces in Canada and there is even a great deal of difficulty when it is in just two or three provinces, because each province has its own method of registering an aircraft and its charges, such as chattel mortgages or conditional sales contracts and agreements.

Aeronautics Act
Some provinces, such as British Columbia, have established a central registry for aircraft. In the case of Ontario and other provinces anybody wishing to register an aircraft would presumably have to search every county court registry in the province to ascertain that there were no charges such as chattel mortgages or conditional sales agreements against the aircraft. The method of registration in a central registry is doubly important in the case of stolen aircraft, because a person could acquire an aircraft that had been stolen and be under the impression that he was obtaining good title. Then when the person who had lost the aircraft found out where it was, he would recover it and presumably the person who bought the aircraft would lose $10,000, or whatever he paid for it, because no doubt the person who sold him the aircraft, would have disappeared.
There is also the possibility of double sale by very smooth talking individuals. I refer to selling the same aircraft twice within a very short period of time. Since there is no central registry system it would be impossible to establish who was the actual owner and presumably there would be interesting litigation as a result of the transaction in order to find out who was the actual owner of the aircraft.
One of the most important matters in this bill is the question of financing. I am relying on my memory, but I think within the last year or two in Canada there has been over $200 million invested in the acquisition of aircraft. In a similar period in the United States the figure is roughly $2.5 billion. In the United States they have had a central aircraft registry since 1938 and I understand from my reading on this subject that their registry has been extremely effective and has done an excellent job.
There have been instances in Canada where people wanted to finance the purchase of aircraft. They have found out that we had no central registry, and the extremely involved procedure necessary in going through the ten provinces, perhaps having to search every county court registry in about half of them and having to search central registries in the remainder, and this has been a very strong factor in discouraging needed financing.
I have endeavoured up to this point, Mr. Speaker, to set out roughly what I think is the objective of this bill and to indicate some of the problems. Perhaps the most obvious question for anybody to ask is: is there any great support for this measure? What is the support behind this piece of legislation? I would first of all like to refer to a resolution

passed by the Canadian bar association at their annual convention in 1956. That resolution reads as follows:
Resolved that appropriate enabling legislation be enacted to establish, as soon as possible, a central Canadian aircraft registry located at Ottawa in order to record title to and all encumbrances against Canadian civil aircraft.
This matter had been discussed by the air law committee of the Canadian bar association at considerable length and as a result of their recommendations and studies the Canadian bar association gave their unanimous endorsement to this proposal. In 1957 the Canadian bar association met at Banff and during their 39th annual meeting in this city another resolution was proposed1. This resolution reads:
Whereas because of the Increasing cost of aircraft outside financing is frequently essential and the task of raising the necessary money is rendered difficult by the absence of any central registry of aircraft where title to aircraft and charges and liens thereon can be registered,
Be it resolved that the Canadian bar association again urge the government of Canada to establish such a registry at an early date.
Again, as late as February of this year the Quebec branch of the Canadian bar association gave the following endorsement to my bill:
Whereas the Quebec subsection of the air law section of the Canadian bar association notes with satisfaction that Bill C-37, relating to the establishment of a central registry for aircraft has been introduced in the House of Commons, under the sponsorship of John A. W. Drysdale, M.P.
And whereas the Canadian bar association has already presented a resolution to the Minister of Justice endorsing the principle of a central registry for aircraft.
Now, therefore, the Quebec branch recommends that the council of the Canadian bar association inform the Minister of Justice of its continued interest in the principle underlying Bill C-37 and suggest to the minister that the said Bill C-37 be referred to the appropriate committee of the House of Commons for further study and report and that the said committee be authorized to request interested persons and organizations to appear before it for the purpose of providing such information relating to the subject matter of the said bill as the committee may deem desirable or necessary.
I have tried, Mr. Speaker, to indicate in detail the interest of people who are active in the legal sphere, who understand the complexity of the situation and understand the effect it is having on aircraft financing and who have on every occasion given their unanimous endorsement to the principle of this bill. I would also say that the British Columbia air law section of the Canadian bar association headed by Mr. Jack Cunningham have also provided me with a great deal of information and support in regard to this bill.
What is the present situation under the air regulations, 1960, of the Aeronautics Act? Section 201 provides:
The minister shall cause a register of aircraft to be maintained in which shall be registered the

names of the owner or owners of every aircraft registered under this part and such other particulars concerning the aircraft as the minister directs.
There have been the suggestions that this particular section is adequate to meet the situation. However I will point out very briefly that this particular section does nothing to establish the identity of the owner but merely provides that certain material be furnished as to the aircraft. It provides for registration of the name of the alleged owner of the aircraft but there is no certification as to the ownership of the aircraft.
I might mention, incidentally, that there is no provision for the registration of any liens or charges against this particular certificate, so that it does not do what this piece of legislation is trying to do. It might assist the committee if I indicated the provinces that have central registries-British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland. The provinces which require county court registration are Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Quebec. In Quebec, of course, the situation is a little different, because a chattel mortgage is not recognized in that province, only a mortgage bond by trust deed which is registered in each of the county courts where the mortgagor has a place of business.
What I feel to be the prime objective of this legislation is to have a single central registry in Ottawa to provide for the compulsory registration of the aircraft, engines, propellers and parts. It should be a registry where there could be a very simple and quick search to ascertain the state of the title to the aircraft and find out what liens and charges are registered against the aircraft.
I made some inquiries in connection with the situation in the United States. The aircraft registry in Washington has been operating successfully since 1938. I had hoped to have a firsthand look at their operations when visiting Washington shortly before Easter, but on my arrival I found they had taken the centralizing step themselves and had moved their offices to Oklahoma city. I understand from discussions with some of the officials in Washington that under the United States system in addition to providing a registry indicating the various charges and the ownership of the aircraft they have, in effect, a complete operation and service record of the aircraft so that an individual making inquiries can find out when the engine has been changed or a new propeller acquired or servicing of the aircraft in addition to ownership and all charges. I suggest that if there were similar facilities here in a central aircraft registry in
Aeronautics Act
Ottawa they would be invaluable as far as expanding aircraft financing in this country is concerned.
There is some question as to the constitutional situation; in other words, whether or not the establishment of a central aircraft registry would be within the powers of parliament under the British North America Act. Just for the record may I say it seems fairly clear that in the Aeronautics Act of 1932 where the privy council upheld the validity of the Aeronautics Act this establishes without question that this particular act is intra vires the powers of parliament. The recent case in 1952 of Johannesson v. Rural Municipality of West St. Paul, I, Supreme Court Reports, 292 lends support to the contention that the protection of security interests is a valid exercise of the powers of the federal government.
In order to confirm this particular viewpoint I engaged in some correspondence with the former minister of transport, now the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I think it would be extremely helpful if I were to put some of his remarks on the record. I wish to do this at length because, as I have indicated, this matter is of extreme importance to the aircraft industry. It is a most technical matter and I hope that making this information available in the pages of Hansard that this will permit the widest possible discussion in the aircraft industry so that we may have both the pros and the cons on this piece of legislation. The letter from the minister of transport is dated April 15, 1959. It reads:
Dear John:
I refer to a previous exchange of correspondence in the matter of the establishment of a central Canadian aircraft registry and in particular to your letter of October 31, 1958, in which the advantages of such a registry to the industry were pointed out.	.
While it would appear to be within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament to provide for the establishment of a registry for liens and encumbrances on aircraft, the existing provisions of the Aeronautics Act would not authorize the making of such regulations and an amendment to the act thereof would be required for the purpose. The wisdom of doing so, however, is in considerable doubt since I am informed that the registration of encumbrances on chattels generally is a matter coming within the jurisdiction of the provinces and that, in fact, such facilities are provided, by the provinces. It may be, however, that these facilities have not been fully employed in the matter of aircraft conveyance.
A federal aircraft registry is in existence in the United States and its function was recently discussed on an informal basis with responsible federal aviation agency officials in Washington. We were somewhat disappointed to find that the complex, time consuming and expensive procedures established by the federal aviation agency have apparently not achieved the original purpose even though the registry has now been expanded to include the recording of conveyances in respect to aircraft engines and even parts. It is understood

Aeronautics Act
that while banks and other loan houses insist upon recording all conveyances respecting aircraft in which they are involved with the federal aviation agency and that the courts are influenced to some extent by the production of such records, these records have not been generally accepted by the courts as evidence of title to the aircraft. The basic difficulty experienced by the federal aviation agency in respect to aircraft title is that resulting from the routine interchangeability of up to four expensive engines and a very large number of extremely expensive airframe and engine components. You will appreciate that, in these circumstances, it would be virtually impossible to say at any given moment who owned a particular aircraft where liens and encumbrances against the airframe itself, individual engines and certain expensive components are held by a number of different persons. It may be of interest to you to know that 12 separate commercial title-searching agencies have been set up in Washington being concerned only with the search of aircraft titles.
While I intend to keep this matter under continuous review, I am not satisfied that it would be either advisable or profitable to set up a federal registry at this time, but will, of course, welcome any further views you may have in the matter.
I have set forth this letter completely. I have done so very frankly because I wanted to present both sides of the picture. The minister has indicated that the amendment which I have contemplated is within the jurisdiction of parliament. He has also indicated why he does not think such a change could be brought about through regulations. It is for that reason I have brought in an amendment to the act. The minister then went to to question the cost of a central aircraft registry and, also the efficacy of a registry of this kind.
I had already written to the federal aviation agency in the United States and they replied to me on November 4, 1960 dealing with my inquiry as to the cost of operating that agency. I do not wish to leave out the cost factor, which I think to be of importance, but we must keep in perspective the relative size of the central aircraft registry in the United States as compared with such a registry in Canada. The letter is dated November 4, 1960 and it is written by Mr. Robert P. Boyle, associate general counsel, general legal services. It says:
Your letter of October 13, 1960 to the administrator of the federal aviation agency was referred to this office for reply.
In that letter you requested information concerning the establishment of a central aircraft registry in Canada. In answer to your specific questions, may I first point out that the following figures are estimates. The interlocking of other functions within the division of this agency, that handles registrations makes it almost impossible to give the exact costs involved. However, the following is a close approximation of the actual figures involved.
Sixty three persons are employed to perform the registration and recordation functions of this agency. The space required is approximately 9,500 square feet. The annual revenue of this function

varies between $190,000 and $215,000. The annual expenditure for support of this function amounts to $350,000.
Although it operates at a slight loss I would suggest that in view of the tremendous cost presently incurred by anyone ascertaining the actual title to an aircraft in Canada it would be possible for the federal government to operate such a registry on a break-even basis.
The former minister of transport indicated in his letter the difficulty existing in this regard particularly in relation to provincial registration. In approaching this aspect of the problem I wrote a letter to each of the attorneys general of the provinces of Canada which I think sets forth clearly the viewpoint I have been trying to express, and I think it would be of value to hon. members if I read this particular letter into the record, following which I shall make reference to some of the replies I have received. I wrote to the attorneys general under date of April 6, 1961, as follows:
Enclosed please find a copy of BUI No. C-37, which seeks to establish a central aircraft registry for the registration of title to and encumbrances against aircraft, aircraft engines, propellers, appliances and spare parts.
At present each province has its own legislation governing the question of title to and encumbrances against aircraft. The present system has actually prevented aircraft financing because of the multiplicity of registries and the searches required to ascertain the state of the title of aicraft in Canada, particularly if the aircraft has been flown in several or all of the provinces.
I am writing to you because, although it appears to be within the legislative Jurisdiction of parliament to provide for the establishment of such a central aircraft registry, in order to make the system effective I think it would require provincial co-operation to the extent that the provinces would require regisration only in the central registry and not under the existing provincial legislation.
I would, therefore, appreciate receiving your comments on the principle of the bill and whether or not you would be prepared to give the necessary co-operation to make such legislation effective.
I should point out that the Canadian bar association is already on record with resolutions supporting the principle of a central aircraft registry. The international air transport association also supports the principle of such a registry, and is, in fact, setting up a study group in conjunction with other organizations to bring in recommendations on this matter. The bill is based on the central aircraft registry provisions named in the United States federal aeronautics act.
I should emphasize that, being a private member's bill, the only discussions will be on the principle of the bill on second reading, but I am hopeful that by bringing it forward for public discussion in the house and indicating the amount of support that is behind the creation of such a registry, the government will give more serious consideration to bringing in the necessary legislation for the establishment of such a registry.
It was interesting to go through some of the replies I received, and I am sure the hon. members will be interested in obtaining this information.

I start out in the far west, in my own province of British Columbia, with the letter I received from Mr. Bonner, the attorney general, dated May 8, 1961 which reads as follows:
Further to my secretary's letter of April 25th, I wish to say that the departmental committee has drawn to my attention certain points which I think you might wish to examine in connection with your proposed bill affecting aircraft registry. For example, section 27 of your bill purports to prohibit the operation or navigation of any aircraft that is not eligible for registration, and it appears that to be eligible for registration the aircraft must be owned by a Canadian citizen. The bill has been examined to see whether, for instance, a major American air line might be exempted from that provision, but no such exception has been included.
If you agree with this interpretation, does it truly represent the policy you would wish to see endorsed?
Second, the registration system proposed by the bill establishes no priority between encumbrancers as a result of registration dates. While there is nothing to be criticized with regard to such a system if it is well and widely understood, encumbrancers having registered charges under present provincial systems here may have a valid objection if the protection that they have gained by taking advantage of provincial legislation to be removed because of the establishment of a central registry such as you proposed.
I should like your reaction to these observations before I attempt to discuss the bill with my colleagues.
Mr. Speaker, I think the objections raised in that letter in connection with the second matter are valid. I might say that I hoped to receive this type of reply to my letters. I think however that objection has been effectively answered by referring to a paper presented by Mr. David I. Johnston, a member of the Quebec bar to the annual meeting of the Quebec branch of the Canadian bar association in 1959. That paper is entitled "Some Legal Aspects of Financing Aircraft Purchases," and at page 14 there appears the following statement:
The matter of the seniority inter se of liens and other security interests in aircraft would appear to be a subject for federal legislation once the registry is established. The unsatisfactory alternative would be to leave an area of uncertainty until the courts evolve a priority of liens from the various provincial statutes and precedents.
Then he draws attention to a proposed revision of section 503 of the United States civil aeronautics act establishing the following ranking:
1.	Court costs
2.	Storage, material men's and repair men's liens
3.	Recorded security interests
4.	Government tax and penalty liens
5.	Unrecorded security interests
As between two liens of the same class, priority would be determined upon a common law time-right basis.
I would suggest such a provision included in the present legislation would clear up the difficulties raised by the attorney general of British Columbia.
90205-6-464
Aeronautics Act
The next letter to which I should like to refer is a reply from the Hon. E. Manning, attorney general of the province of Alberta, dated April 24, 1961 which reads as follows:
I am in receipt of your letter of April 6th together with a copy of Bill No. C-37.
In this province as you are no doubt aware, we have a central registry in relation to aircraft which seems to be working out quite satisfactorily.
In so far as this province is concerned, we have had no request for a central aircraft registry applicable to the whole of the dominion and I am not prepared to make any comments on the proposal outlined in Bill No. C-37.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that by drawing the attention of the house to some of the unfavourable as well as the favourable comments that interested individuals in the various provinces will contact the various attorneys general to indicate support for this legislation.
The next reply to which I would like to refer is from the attorney general of Manitoba, the Hon. Sterling R. Lyon dated June 2, 1961, which reads as follows:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of April 6. 1961, relative to the registration of title to aircraft, etc. I much regret that, due to the fact that your letter was received during the session of the legislature and to pressure of other matters since, I have been unable to reply earlier.
I am personally in accord with your view that any really practicable system of registration of aircraft should be established by act of parliament. I would think, from consideration of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Johannesson v. Rural Municipality of West St. Paul (1952) I, S.C.R. 292, that there is no doubt that parliament, if deemed advisable, may properly enact such legislation.
I agree that to make any such legislation fully effective, it would be necessary to enact complementary provincial legislation forbidding registration of aircraft under provincial statutes. It seems to me that, in so far as Manitoba is concerned, this might be achieved simply by amending the definition of "chattels" in clause (b) of subsection (1) of section 2 of the bills of sale act, so as to exclude aircraft or parts thereof, in a manner similar to that in which ships registered under the Canada Shipping Act or the merchants shipping act, 1894 (Imperial), are excluded.
If the parliament of Canada should pass legislation that appears to me to achieve the purposes mentioned in your letter, I would be prepared to canvass this matter among those interested in our province and, subject to there being reasonable evidence of support among aircraft owners and others affected here, to recommend to the executive council of Manitoba that a bill for the required complementary legislation above mentioned be considered for enactment.
This one is more favourable than those from some of the other attorneys general.
Then we pass on to the province of Ontario. The Hon. Kelso Roberts, the attorney general, wrote to me as follows, and made what I thought was an excellent suggestion.
With reference to your letter of the 6th of April, 1961, which was referred by me on its receipt to Mr. Elliott R. Pepper, Q.C., departmental counsel, for study.

Aeronautics Act
Mr. Pepper in return discussed it with the deputy attorney general and they feel that this is a question which might well be discussed by the uniformity commissioners composed, as you are no doubt aware, of the deputy attorneys general of all provinces and certain other personnel, and which committee meets for one week immediately prior to the week of the Canadian bar association annual meeting. This year the commissioners will be meeting in Regina.
You might consider it advisable to discuss the matter with the Minister of Justice and if you both feel that this procedure is advisable I am sure that the Minister of Justice can arrange to have the matter placed on the agenda for discussion by the commissioners this summer.
I might say for the benefit of the house that I have written such a letter to the Minister of Justice drawing the matter to his attention.
The next reply that I received was from the assistant deputy attorney general of the province of Quebec. In that letter dated April 27, 1961, he wrote to me as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am directed by the honourable the attorney general to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 6th instant concerning the establishment of a central aircraft registry.
We understand that pursuant to section IV of the Aeronautics Act, the registration of aircrafts is actually a matter of regulations made by the Minister of Transport.
With regard to this particular suggestion, with respect, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I think the former minister of transport has indicated quite clearly that the regulations cannot be utilized to extend them to the extent that the assistant deputy attorney general suggests.
It may seem like this is a political tour of the provinces, but the next letter is from the attorney general of the province of New Brunswick, the Hon. Louis J. Robichaud, who wrote me as follows:
Dear Mr. Drysdale:
I wish to acknowledge with thanks your letter of April 6th enclosing copy of Bill No. C-37, an act to amend the Aeronautics Act.
There is no legislation in this province having specific reference to the title to and encumbrances against aircraft.
I would prefer not to comment on the merits of the bill at this time.
With regard to the other attorneys general, I sent follow-up notes to see if I could get some comments from them because I feel that this particular suggested legislation is sufficiently important to justify a completely thorough review of the assistance their answers would provide.
I should now like to turn very briefly, if I may, to the international aspects of this particular legislation. As I indicated in the explanatory notes to the bill, I was interested in having a central registry to comply with the provisions of the convention on the international recognition of rights in aircraft.

Perhaps, because not all hon. members are familiar with this particular piece of legislation, I should put it in a very brief summary. I would commend to the house the source material which I have used which is an historical survey of the law of flight put out by the institute of air and space law, McGill University, Montreal, 1961.
The objectives are set out on page 38 of this survey as follows:
The general objective of the convention-
This is the one that I have already referred to sometimes called the Geneva convention, or the mortgage convention.
The general objective of this convention is the facilitation of the financing of aircraft employed in international carriage. More specifically, the objectives can be said to be four: the protection of secured creditors who lend money on the security of aircraft; the protection of third parties dealing in or with aircraft against hidden charges; the definition and protection of "privileged" and "priority" claims against aircraft; and the facilitation of the transfer of aircraft from one nationality to another.
To achieve these objectives, the convention could have taken one of two forms. It could have created a standard form of mortgage and transfer for use in all contracting states, having uniform effect in all jurisdictions, or it could have provided foir the recognition and enforcement by contracting states of any type of charge created in accordance with the law of the state in which the aircraft is registered as to nationality. Unfortunately, the first solution proved unattainable. The divergence in national conceptions proved too great at the time for an adequate compromise standard to be reached. Thus, the convention became a convention not of unification but of recognition.
An attempt was then made to produce an internationally acceptable form of words to cover all the types of charges on aircraft or, more accurately, rights in aircraft to be recognized by contracting states. This was found to be impossible and so an enumeration of four types of rights was resorted to. These are rights of property in aircraft; rights to acquire aircraft by purchase coupled with possession of the aircraft; rights to possession of aircraft under leases of six months or more; mortgages, hypotheques and similar rights in aircraft which are contractually created as security for payment of an indebtedness.
The United States has ratified this particular convention and I would suggest that it would be in the interest of Canada, first of all giving support and recognition to ICAO, which has its headquarters in Montreal, and also giving support to this particular convention, for it is only by establishing a central registry that we will be in a position to ratify this very important convention.
Perhaps I can close, Mr. Speaker, by summarizing very briefly. There is every indication of a widespread interest in aviation and financial circles for the creation of such an aircraft registry. I have pointed out quite clearly that the federal government has the legislative power, which is backed up by the case law and also by the acknowledgment of the former minister of transport.

I indicated earlier that, so far as the provinces are concerned you should not have the situation of duplicate legislation. Without provincial co-operation, they will be free to insist that the title to mortgages, conditional sales agreements, and so forth, be registered in the provinces in addition to the central registry. I have tried to set up discussion machinery to meet this particular point by communicating with the various attorneys general.
I would recommend, sir, that two or three steps be considered. The first step would be, I think, that there would have to be reference to the uniformity commissioners at the meeting of the deputy attorneys general in Regina to get the necessary support of the various provinces. Perhaps the most effective way of doing this would be for the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Transport to present draft legislation perhaps modeled on the legislation I have already proposed in Bill No. C-37.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the sponsor of this bill although I had some difficulty in hearing many of the things he said. I listened with keen interest for a time, and then I got lost when he put on the record so much correspondence between himself and the former minister of transport and then between himself and the attorneys general. I am sure that what I have said thus far will not indicate to him that I am being unfair to the bill.
I have looked at the bill, sir, and I have certain doubts about it which I think should be emphasized to the house at this time. The purpose of Bill No. C-37 as outlined in the explanatory note is to provide a central Canadian aircraft registry, preferably in Ottawa-I think the hon. member said in Ottawa-in order to record title to and all encumbrances against Canadian civil aircraft. Two or three queries come to my mind as I read the explanatory note.
The first has to do with jurisdiction. I have some doubts in my mind whether an enactment of this kind would be intra vires of the parliament of Canada. It is true that the former minister of transport in his letter to the hon. member indicated, I believe, that there was no objection from that standpoint but nevertheless I should like to bring to the attention of the house the fact that in the new section 26(1) the bill deals with (a) any conveyance which affects the title to, or any interest in, any civil aircraft; (b) any 90205-6-464J
Aeronautics Act
lease, and any mortgage, contract of conditional sale or other instrument and (c) any lease, and any mortgage, contract of conditional sale or other instrument, with certain other qualifications. This immediately leads me to the point whether or not this does not invade the field of property and civil rights.
I should like to bring this fact to the attention of the house. At one stage parliament gave the Minister of Transport authority to amend the Aeronautics Act so as to cover the zoning of airports and the zoning regulations had to be drafted very carefully so that they would not impinge in any way upon municipal jurisdiction. In fact, the first draft came very close to that and, if I remember correctly, the regulations had to be redrafted on one if not on two different occasions.
That is what strikes me about this bill as I look at it. In order not to impede the legislation in any way, may I tell the hon. member at once that I have not risen to oppose the bill. I wish to raise certain doubts that are in my mind about its validity.
The first point that I raise is that this is special legislation and legislation of this character should be very carefully worded because, as I said earlier, it might well impinge upon the jurisdiction of the provinces.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Would he agree with the principle of the bill, the establishment of a central registry? I must confess that I am not entirely happy with many of the words myself that involve details but I am interested in whether or not he is in accord with the principle of the legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: I should have liked to come to that a little later but if my friend wants an answer now may I say that I would prefer to take the position taken by the Quebec branch of the Canadian bar association, which my hon. friend seemed to think indicated approval. As I heard him read the recommendation it was to the effect that the Quebec branch of the Canadian bar association recommends continuing interest in this bill and further recommends that it be referred to the appropriate committee for study, or words to that effect. I can see absolutely nothing the matter with that kind of resolution and I would go all the way in supporting it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
May I draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that they did not disapprove of the principle of a central aircraft registry. They may have had some reservations as to the wording of the

Aeronautics Act
bill, which was taken, quite frankly, from the United States legislation, but they did not disapprove of the principle.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
I would not even want to go that far until I knew more about the position, and I will tell the hon. member why. If it is so, as I fear, that the bill might be an impingement upon the right of a province to have registered within the province a conveyance, a chattel mortgage, although as the hon. member rightly said there are no chattel mortgages in the province of Quebec, a lease, a mortgage and so on, I would not in that event give the bill approval in principle.
That is why I think we should have two things so far as this bill is concerned. First, as is customary we should have the opinion of the minister. What does the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) think about this legislation? Second, we should be informed whether or not the Minister of Transport has submitted the bill to the Department of Justice to ascertain whether or not it is an infringement of property and civil rights.
When the hon. member posed his question I was going to discuss another matter, the ability or facility of the Department of Transport to administer legislation of this kind. Can it be done? Can it be done easily or can it be done only with great difficulty? These are questions on which I think we require enlightenment from the Department of Transport.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Does he feel that there would be more difficulty in the administration of this legislation than with regard to the present shipping registry provisions which are under the Department of Transport?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: I think there would be a great deal more than in the case of the present shipping registration.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
I do not see any difficulty with regard to the present shipping registry. During all the time that I was on that side of the house acting in the capacity of the present Minister of Transport I never had any complaint so far as the registry of ships was concerned. There may have been some since. After having looked at these various sections, particularly 26 and 27, I think there would likely be greater difficulty in administration. I am not saying that it is not feasible or possible. What I am saying is that on the face of the bill and without knowing more

about it than I do it would strike me that it would be rather difficult to administer this kind of legislation.
All these doubts might disappear if the bill were referred to a committee for study and the committee heard evidence from the various persons concerned, particularly from the officials of the Department of Transport. I should like to know what the officials, particularly the legal advisers and the heads of the various aviation divisions of the department, think about this legislation.
I would not want the hon. member to feel that I rose for the purpose of opposing the bill because I know he has put a lot of time and effort into its preparation. That can be seen from the lengthy correspondence which he put on the record and which it will be possible to read carefully tomorrow or later. But before giving my support to the bill, and I speak now only for myself, I would want to know, first, whether it is intra vires of the parliament of Canada, second, whether it can be easily administered and, third, whether it is special legislation. In order to get answers to these three questions I think the minister should be here to tell us how he and those with whom he is associated in the department view this legislation. Until then I would rather reserve my comments.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman one question before he sits down, and that is in connection with the question of the legislation being intra vires the powers of parliament?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
The former minister of
transport, as I indicated, had received an opinion from the justice department indicating that this was intra vires the powers of the federal government. In addition, I might also say to the hon. member that all the authorities that I have seen that have been actively associated with the field of air law and interested in this particular type of legislation, have given the opinion based on these two cases that it was intra vires. I wonder if the hon. member has any specific instances going in the contrary direction because if there are it would be helpful to know about them in overcoming this difficulty. I have not seen any, and I was wondering if the hon. member had seen any.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
Dealing first with the former minister's opinion, it is my belief the minister was giving his personal opinion only to the hon. member who introduced this bill. He was not speaking as the minister for the department. While he did say that he had consulted his officers, I think the proper method by which to obtain an opinion as to

whether legislation is intra vires of parliament is to get it from the Department of Justice. This, the minister did not do.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: I want to correct that statement. The minister did obtain an opinion from the Department of Justice, and then passed on that opinion in his letter. He had obtained it from the Department of Justice because I had raised the question in previous correspondence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
I had not understood that to be the case as the hon. member read his letter. However, I shall read the letter tomorrow. None the less, I think we should have a repetition of that statement by the present minister because, after all, the former minister is no longer the minister and no longer responsible for the administration of the department.
The hon. member wanted to know if I knew of any case in which there was some doubt or hesitation about a matter such as this, because, after all, we could probably conciliate the two views. Yes, I do, and I did mention it a moment ago in connection with the zoning regulations. The zoning regulations came very nearly to impinging on provincial jurisdiction. I say now that these had to be drafted and redrafted on several occasions because as they were worded and as they were drafted in the first instance they seemed to many of us who were lawyers to be an infringement of provincial jurisdiction. This is the question mark I have in my mind at the moment, that this might well be an impingement upon the rights of the provinces in the field of property and civil rights.
As a result of the doubt which I have in my mind, and which with all respect to the former minister of transport, I still have, I raised these queries and thought that perhaps the best thing to do under the circumstances would be to refer the bill to a committee where the officers of the department as well as the Department of Justice could give their views on the validity of the legislation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes that are left I should like to place a few of my views on the record. I listened most intently to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale). He is certainly to be congratulated upon having done a monumental job. If it had not been for the rules of the house I think he would have achieved an even more monumental accomplishment by talking out his own bill. He has given a true evaluation of this bill in that he has said it is the most important enactment to be brought before this house as a private member's bill.
Business of the House
I will agree with him, perhaps, with the exception of three or four bills which stand in my name.
It may be that the information he has put on the record, not only as a result of his own research but also the letters directed to the various attorneys general of the provinces with whom he has corresponded, will give valuable information to the Department of Transport and the Department of Justice. I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I have not the faintest idea which particular department should look after this matter. However, whichever department does, there will be information on the record for their guidance. I was rather struck by the extent to which an hon. member will go in trying to bring out points in favour of his bill. I do recognize, Mr. Speaker, that I seconded this bill but I did so only for the purpose of bringing it before the house. I did not want the house to act in the same manner as the other place where hon. members' bills have died because no one would bring them before the other place. I think every member has a right to have his bill come before the house at the proper time and receive full consideration.
The hon. member made a great point of the mobility of airplanes. He did point out that we have registries in the various provinces for motor vehicles. Not being a lawyer, I somehow assumed the motorcar to be almost equal in mobility to that of the airplane, that what would apply to one vehicle would apply to the other. He also pointed out the dollar value of the sales of airplanes, some $200 million in Canada. He said he was relying on his memory for this figure, but it does seem to be a good, round sum. However, I would suspect that the greater part of it is made up of sales of commercial airplanes. I cannot see anybody running away with a Viscount or a DC-8. It seems to me that if you took out the sales of commercial planes, this figure would drop down to a point where, although not insignificant, it would not be of the major importance the hon. member has tried to make it appear.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: It includes commercial aircraft.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: That is what I say; a central registry of commercial aircraft is not going to be of much value-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE CANADIAN AIRCRAFT REGISTRY
speechtext: Order; I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but it is my duty to do so, it being six o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before asking the minister for the business of the house, I should like to remind him that he has been

Business of the House
asking those of us who sit on this side for co-operation in the last few days, and even for some time prior to that. We have been giving it to him. I should like to suggest to him that it would be much easier for all concerned if he could indicate clearly what the business of the house is going to be, what the government proposes to do tomorrow and for the whole of next week as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that there is a general desire to expedite the business of the house at this time of year. However, it has not been possible to get full agreement on all matters. There has been an understandable difference of opinion between this side of the house and the other side as to what should be proceeded with on a particular day.
However, it is fairly clear now that if it is the desire of the house to adjourn soon and reassemble later in the fall, certain matters should be completed within the next few days if at all possible so that we leave things in good order during a short recess.
Under the circumstances, we intend tomorrow, Saturday, to take the estimates of the departments of public works, forestry, defence production and health and welfare. If good progress is made with these departments, we could make a start on national revenue.
On Monday and Tuesday we have available for consideration Bill No. C-92 which has come back from the Senate with a proposed amendment. That is the capital murder bill. Then the Excise Act, the Customs Tariff Act, the Industrial Development Bank Act, the Excise Tax Act and the C.N.R. financing resolution to be followed by an appropriation bill.
Those latter items have not come from the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, just the first one that I mentioned. On the order paper there is also the Civil Service Act with which the house might wish to deal in view of the lengthy discussion it has had in committee. Then there is the Bank of Canada Act to be considered, the Customs Tariff Act which has been returned from the Senate-that is Bill No. C-72-and the final act following the budget, the Income Tax Act. Then there would be some supplementary estimates and interim supply to be considered before an adjournment.
It looks like September.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is a possibility of the dominion-provincial tax sharing arrangements resolution being considered by the house, if it is agreeable.

I will announce tomorrow the exact order of those items on Monday and Tuesday, but of those items there is one, the Bank of Canada Act, which will definitely come up on Tuesday. That is the business, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house
leader will remember that the Prime Minister has repeatedly stated that estimates would not be taken up on Saturday.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
The house leader said that last night.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When there was a discussion of the motion to extend the hours it was clearly stated that we would not have estimates on Saturday, and again last night. The question was put to the house leader by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as reported at page 7298 of Hansard:
Would the minister say whether this program will go on for Saturday as well or could he indicate what would be happening on Saturday?
Will estimates be taken on Saturday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No-
That was last night.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a categorical statement that estimates would not be taken on Saturday.
I didn't think so, at this late stage of the session.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There are a number of matters which could be disposed of and in which the opposition would be quite willing to co-operate in so far as legislation is concerned. The house leader mentioned the agreement-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think a word of explanation is required. When I said last night that estimates would not be taken up on Saturday I was under the impression at that time that we would be able to go ahead with certain of the bills following the budget. But there was no agreement to that course whatsoever when the discussion was held this morning.
The second point is that on April 24 when the Prime Minister was discussing the lengthening of the hours he made a definite commitment which I should have remembered at that time. The Prime Minister said that Saturdays would be set aside for dealing with the supply of various departments. These are his exact words, as reported at page 3928 of Hansard:
On Saturdays various departments could be dealt with. I would not want to see controversial measures dealt with on Saturdays-

In view of that commitment, it seems wise to proceed with the discussion of estimates tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, will the house leader not consider the advisability of proceeding tomorrow with a bill of immediate urgency and importance, the Bank of Canada Act, so that we can deal with that at once, because the Minister of Finance stressed last Monday how important it is to get this through with a minimum of delay; that it involved what he called a crisis.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I can understand the desire of the opposition to proceed with that particular bill. I wish they had shown the same desire with regard to the bills that followed the budget and we perhaps might have come to some agreement with regard to a legislative program on Saturday.
We did.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That agreement was not reached and therefore I think we had better keep to the commitment made by the Prime Minister on April 24 to reserve Saturdays for the discussion of estimates.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I asked for the business of the house last night and I clearly understood that the minister gave us an assurance that the estimates would not be taken on Saturday. There was no qualification of that whatsoever. When the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked: "Will estimates be taken on Saturday?" the minister said, "No", and he made no qualification of that.
And he referred to interim supply for a two-month period.

I might add that when the Prime Minister asked for our co-operation last Monday he indicated clearly what measures would have to be passed before we adjourned, and he did not include any estimates in that group. This is a repudiation both of what the Prime Minister said on Monday and of the express word of the house leader given to me last night.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member for Kootenay West should speak before the minister.

Mr. Speaker, I support wholeheartedly the proposal made by the Leader of the Opposition and the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Business of the House
In this respect we are two parties with one objective, to conclude the work of this session as soon as possible.
This government is leaderless. They have not even got their bills before us on tax matters.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
In the opinion of certain members of the young Liberals association it may soon be one party. What I said yesterday was this:
The intention will be to complete, in so far as we can, the resolutions and the bills following the budget.
That was for today:
If the house passes the resolutions tomorrow,-
That is, Friday:
-as has now been indicated, then of course, I think the bills would normally follow on Saturday.
Read the rest of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It was then that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised a very serious objection, and I said after he raised this objection:
-and the bills on Monday?
That was apparently what he wanted, whereas we wanted to have the tax bills on Saturday. Without the agreement that is necessary we might just as well follow the course that has been followed now for the last several weeks and keep to the commitment made on April 24 that estimates be taken on Saturday.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of this measure and the attempt we are all making to finish the business of the session at this stage, I ask the Minister of Finance does he not think, in view of the statements he has made regarding the importance of the Bank of Canada Act, that he owes to the house and to the country an explanation for the postponement that he and the government have authorized with regard to this matter? This puts the minister in a most humiliating position and he owes the nation an explanation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It seems to me that the discussion of the business of the house is now taking the form of a debate. If the Minister of Finance does not wish to reply, I will leave the chair and adjourn the house.

Just a big majority steamrolling; that is all it is.
It being ten minutes after six o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Questions
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Was Canadian flour made available free of charge to the government of Chile in 1960 for the relief of disaster victims?
2.	If so: (a) what was the amount involved? (b) what was the total cost to Canada?
3.	Have any reports been noted by the Canadian embassy in Chile to the effect that: (a) this flour was being trafficked for political purposes instead of being given free to disaster victims; (b) a prominent Chilean politician has been arrested for allegedly dealing in Canadian flour?
4.	If so, has the Canadian government made any representations ?
5.	If so, what are their nature?
Answer by: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary
of State for External Affairs):
1.	Yes.
2.	(a) 9,832 long tons, (b) $999,864.48.
3.	(a) There were such reports in some newspapers but to the best of our knowledge they are not accurate and were refuted by the government, (b) It has been reported that Mr. S. C. Gonzales was arrested for falsely accusing the government of malpractice.
4.	No.
5.	Not applicable.
